text:
🔴Iran Offers U.S. Seven-Day Plan to Reopen Strait of Hormuz as Diplomacy Intensifies

📍NEW YORK, September 25, 2026 , HewadPress:— Iran has presented the United States with what Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described as a “concrete” seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as diplomatic efforts intensify on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday that Tehran believes the framework is ready to be implemented if Washington agrees to the necessary steps.

“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said, adding that the decision now rests with Washington. 

Araghchi said the measures Tehran is asking the United States to take are not new, arguing that they are already contained in the Memorandum of Understanding, or MoU, reached between Washington and Tehran in June.

“All those actions that the United States should take are not new,” Araghchi said. “They are all already in the MoU.”

According to the Associated Press, Iran’s latest proposal calls for the United States to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions restricting Iranian oil sales and observe a ceasefire that would also cover Lebanon. Iran would then reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart negotiations with Washington over its nuclear program. 

Araghchi said the seven-day timetable would begin once Washington accepts the proposal. Under the plan he outlined, initial measures would be implemented during the first several days, the strait would reopen by around the sixth day, and negotiations toward a broader agreement would begin on the seventh day. 
The proposal comes amid renewed diplomatic contacts surrounding the U.N. General Assembly.

Qatar has been playing a mediating role between Washington and Tehran, while U.S. and Iranian representatives have exchanged messages through intermediaries during talks in New York. Both sides have described recent contacts in relatively positive terms, although no breakthrough has been announced. 

Earlier this week, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington remained open to talks with Iranian officials if negotiations could produce meaningful progress.

Rubio said the central U.S. objective remains preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. 

Following the latest contacts, however, Rubio cautioned against describing the diplomatic discussions as a breakthrough. He also accused Iran of violating the June MoU, illustrating the continuing disagreement between Washington and Tehran over why the previous arrangement collapsed. 

Iran, meanwhile, argues that Washington has obligations under that earlier agreement that could provide the foundation for a new deal.

Hormuz at center of negotiations

The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the most important bargaining points in efforts to end the conflict. Before the war, roughly one-fifth of globally traded oil and gas passed through the strategic waterway, making disruption there a major concern for international energy markets. 

Iran has previously said it could restore normal passage through the strait within a week if Washington eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports. A senior Iranian official told Reuters earlier this week that Tehran’s delegation in New York had authority to pursue a diplomatic agreement with Washington. 

The latest proposal therefore represents one of the clearest publicly outlined Iranian offers in recent months: reciprocal measures over seven days, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and then returning to negotiations over a broader settlement.

But significant disagreements remain, particularly over sanctions, the U.S. naval presence and Iran’s nuclear program.

For now, Tehran says the framework is ready. Washington has expressed openness to diplomacy but has not publicly accepted Iran’s seven-day proposal.

text:
The Nicopolis massacre refers to the mass execution of thousands of Christian crusader prisoners by Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I in September 1396, following the Battle of Nicopolis. The incident cemented Ottoman dominance in the Balkans, and halted large-scale Western European military interventions against the Turks for over a century.... 

On September 25, 1396, one of the greatest Christian armies assembled during the late Middle Ages was destroyed beside the Danube. The battle was terrible. But what happened the following morning was worse.

The prisoners were brought before the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I with ropes around their bodies. Many had been stripped. Knights, archers, servants, and wounded soldiers were forced into lines beneath the eyes of the man they called the Thunderbolt.

Then the killing began.

Only the wealthy and politically valuable could hope to survive. They could be ransomed. The ordinary soldiers, however, had nothing to offer.

So Bayezid watched as they were beheaded.

Among the prisoners was Johann Schiltberger, a sixteen-year-old Bavarian who had accompanied his knightly master on crusade. He had survived the battle only to find himself bound to two other captives and driven before the sultan. The men beside him were killed. Schiltberger was spared because of his youth.

He would never forget what he saw.

. . .

The disaster had begun with a desperate appeal from Eastern Europe. The Ottoman Empire was advancing through the Balkans. Christian kingdoms had fallen or been reduced to vassalage. Countless had been dragged away to feed the insatiable hunger of the Islamic slave markets. Even Constantinople was under pressure. Hungary now stood dangerously exposed.

So King Sigismund of Hungary called for help.

French and Burgundian knights answered. So did Germans, Hungarians, Wallachians, Hospitallers, and warriors from across Christian Europe. They crossed the Danube carrying banners, armor, and absolute confidence. They believed Bayezid would flee at the news of their approach.

He did not flee.

The crusading army reached Nicopolis, a heavily fortified Ottoman stronghold in present-day Bulgaria, and began a siege.

Bayezid raced north to meet them with reinforcements.

King Sigismund understood the Ottoman way of war. He urged the French knights to wait and allow the more lightly armed Wallachians to test the enemy’s lines. But the French refused. They had traveled too far, spent too much, and dreamed too long of glory to surrender the honor of the first charge. Their armored cavalry thundered forward.

At first, the attack appeared unstoppable. The knights smashed through the Ottoman front ranks and drove uphill beneath clouds of arrows. But Bayezid had placed sharpened stakes before his deeper infantry lines. Horses fell. Knights were thrown into the dust. Others dismounted and continued on foot, burdened by armor and exhausted by the climb.

When they reached the ridge, they discovered that the army they thought they had defeated was still waiting for them. Ottoman cavalry closed around their flanks.

The French fought savagely, but they were isolated. When Sigismund advanced with the remaining Christian forces, Serbian cavalry serving as Ottoman vassals struck his army and helped break it apart.

The crusade completely collapsed. Men fled toward the Danube. Some drowned beneath the weight of their armor. Others reached the ships only to find them overcrowded. Schiltberger later wrote that desperate men clinging to the vessels were beaten away and left to disappear beneath the water.

Sigismund escaped. But thousands did not.

When Bayezid surveyed the battlefield and saw the bodies of his soldiers, he ordered the Christian prisoners brought before him the following day. What followed was a calculated massacre of bound men. The executions continued for hours.

text:
STALINGRAD
——————-
* The changing of the guard at the Stalingrad memorial.

Stalingrad. Some have heard the name, a vague recollection from a documentary aired on television or a white title seen standing out on the black cover of a large-format monograph in a downtown bookstore.

Stalingrad, however, deserves better than that. It is the place where the Soviets put an end to the dominating aspirations of a deranged assailant. A city in which every square inch became the object of a mortal struggle between the Germans and the Russians. Eight agonizing months, from July 1942 to February 1943, during which the men of the East obeyed Stalin to the letter: “Not one step back,” he had commanded them. The Red Army fatally broke the will of the Reich; the Germans never recovered from their defeat in the face of Russian determination.

Fast-forward to 2022.

Immediately after the debilitating pandemic of our era, the coalesced Young Global Leaders of the West bared their chests before Putin with an arrogance that struck me as unconscious from the outset. “But what are they doing, for heaven’s sake?” I thought. I knew the history and Russia’s contributions during the Second World War, having read Winston Churchill’s autobiography when I was younger. We had succeeded in 1989 in melting the Cold War for good, and now, after the health scam of the century, the globo-totalitarian protagonists wanted to open the freezer in order to bury Putin and his people. I was stunned. “Are you mad?” I thought. The Russians halted Hitler’s advances in the East and were the first, ahead of the others, to set foot in Berlin on 21 April 1945 to extinguish all the Nazi dictator’s hopes. They raised the Soviet flag on the mast of the Reichstag.

The Russians lost nearly 500,000 men at Stalingrad; but they sacrificed 26,600,000 people in total to bring down the Nazi regime. The Russians do not let go. They see things through. This is not praise I offer them, but rather an observation I share.

What ruined my faith in the West, in February 2022, was the realization that my fellow citizens, ordinary men and women, stupid and easily manipulated, replaced one scam with another without blinking; no knowledge of history, no humility acting as a sense of propriety on a subject about which they had strictly no reason to take one side rather than another. But the Russians—what had they done to them to become their mortal enemies in this way? Suddenly it was acceptable to fleece citizens in order to send billions of dollars in an unbroken chain, drawn from their own pockets, to drop bombs on the head of the bear 7,000 km away, from Montreal to Moscow. It was imperative to meddle in affairs at the other end of the world with Ukrainian flag emojis. Unspeakable damned misery…

text:
STALINGRAD
——————-
* La passation de la garde au mémorial de Stalingrad.

Stalingrad. Certains on entendu le nom, un vague souvenir ouï lors d’un documentaire diffusé à la télé ou un titre blanc vu en exergue sur la couverture noir d’une monographie grand-format dans une librairie du centre-ville.

Stalingrad, pourtant, mérite mieux que ça. C’est là où les soviétiques mirent fin aux aspirations dominatrices d’un assaillant dément. Une ville où chaque pouce carré fit l’objet d’une lutte mortelle entre les allemands et les russes. Huit mois agonisants, de juillet 42 à février 43, pendant lesquels les hommes de l’est obéirent à Stalin à la lettre : « pas un pas derrière » leur avait-il commandé. L’armée rouge brisa la volonté du Reich fatalement ; jamais les allemands ne se remirent de leur perte face à la détermination russe.

Fast-forward 2022

Immédiatement suivant la pandémie débilitante de notre ère, les Young Global Leaders coalisés de l’Occident se dépoitraillèrent face à Poutine avec une arrogance qui m’apparut inconsciente dès le départ. « Mais que font-ils, pour l’amour du ciel ? » pensai-je. Je connaissait l’histoire et les contributions de la Russie au cours de la Deuxième Guerre Mondiale ayant lu, plus jeune, l’autobiographie de Winston Churchill. Nous avions réussi en 1989 à faire fondre pour de bon la Guerre Froide et voilà que débilement, suite à l’arnaque sanitaire du siècle, les protagonistes mondialo-totalitaires voulaient ouvrir le congélateur pour y enfouir Poutine et son peuple. Je fus abasourdi. « Mais vous êtes malades ? » pensai-je. Les Russes stoppèrent les avancées de Hitler dans l’Est, et mirent les pieds, les premiers et donc avant les autres, à Berlin le 21 avril 1945 pour éteindre tous les espoirs du dictateur Nazi. Ils hissèrent le drapeau soviétique sur le mat du Reichstag.

Les russes perdirent près de 500,000 hommes à Stalingrad ; mais ils sacrifièrent 26,600,000 personnes au total pour venir à bout du régime Nazi. Les russes ne lâchent rien. Ils vont au bout des choses. Ce n’est pas une louange que je leur porte mais plutôt un constat que je partage.

Mais ce qui ruina ma foi en l’Occident, en février 2022, fut de constater que mes concitoyens, monsieur et madame tout-le-monde, bêtes et faciles à manipuler, remplacèrent une arnaque avec une autre sans cligner des yeux ; aucune connaissance de l’histoire, aucune humilité faisant acte de pudeur sur un sujet pour lequel il n’avaient strictement aucune raison de prendre un parti plutôt qu’un autre. Mais les russes, que leur avaient-ils fait pour devenir ainsi leurs ennemis mortels ? Soudainement, il était acceptable de détrousser les citoyens pour envoyer des milliards de dollars à la chaîne, tirés de leur propre poche, pour aller lancer des bombes sur la tête de l’ours à 7,000 km, de Montréal à Moscou. Il fallait impérativement se mêler d’affaires à l’autre bout du monde à coup d’emogi de drapeau ukrainien. Esti de misère innommable…

Et là, cerise sur le sundae, Trudeau et sa bande de perdus célébrèrent au Parlement canadien au mois de septembre 2023, sous les applaudissements d’un Zelenskyy ahuri, l’improbable Yaroslav Hunka, un ukrénien Nazi, qui appartenait donc jadis aux dangereux malades du Luftwaffe.

Alors… mes chers followers sur X, ceux qui encore me lisez à l’occasion, et à toi, algorithme maudit qui limite ma portée auprès d’eux, et vous autres, ceux qui m’espionnent sans se commettre parce que c’est dans l’air du temps de faire ainsi, prenez bien note d’une chose : mener une guerre contre la Russie n’est pas une bonne idée. Elle n’est même pas acceptable. Cela équivaudrait à éveiller des morts Stalingrad, reposant dans sa tombe sous l’ombre de la Mère Patrie qui l’appelle. 

Cessez de vous laissez jouer telles des gerbilles par les Young Global Leaders et compagnie qui ne veulent que leur propre bien.

Cessez d’agir comme des criss d’épais qui pensent tout connaitre mais qui en réalité ne savent que très peu de choses.

text:
IRAN SAYS IT CAN REOPEN THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ IN 7 DAYS - THE CONDITIONS ARE WASHINGTON'S TO MEET, NOT TEHRAN'S.

Iran's FM Abbas Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York (Sept 25) that "if the necessary conditions are met," Hormuz "can reopen, normal shipping restored, in seven days." He said the steps needed from the US "aren't new" - they're already written into the June MOU. Sources close to Iran's delegation describe the sequence: days 1-4/5, US lifts the naval blockade on Iranian oil ports and restores export waivers; day 6, Iran opens the strait via the Oman-Iran corridor; day 7, civil nuclear talks begin - compressed from the 60 days set out in the original June deal. Nothing here is signed. This is Iran's offer, still sitting on Washington's desk.

Separately: Xi's Washington visit wrapped Sept 25 with the tariff truce extended to Jan 10, 2027. SCMP also reports (via US Trade Rep Jamieson Greer) that both sides have agreed a "Board of Trade" mechanism and plan to announce Monday a set of less-sensitive goods categories, each side capping tariff cuts around $30B. Still SCMP's account of Greer's comments, not a White House text.

Perspective: about 20% of the world's oil and LNG transits Hormuz, so a real reopening is first an energy-price and shipping-insurance story, not just a diplomatic one. The gap between "conditions already exist in a June MOU" and "actually implemented" has burned this process before - Araghchi says he's twice heard Washington call talks "productive," then watched the US strike the next day. Whether Hormuz opens looks less like a Tehran decision and more like a Washington sequencing problem: who moves first. If it holds, it shows up in oil, freight and insurance pricing before it shows up in any headline. Not a signal to trade any asset on - just the mechanics worth watching this week.

Not financial advice - information only.

Iran has offered what it calls a path toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending hostilities. But today we learned something rather important about what Tehran apparently believes “negotiation” means. According to Reuters, a senior Iranian official says Iran will make no concessions on its nuclear program, even if the United States accepts Tehran’s Hormuz proposal. Iran also says the Strait will remain closed until all of its conditions are met. Those conditions are substantial. Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian funds and waive sanctions on Iranian oil. Iran would then reopen Hormuz, while nuclear negotiations would come later. 

There is also an interesting contradiction developing inside Tehran. President Masoud Pezeshkian has publicly indicated Iran could dilute its 60-percent enriched uranium stockpile and permit international verification. Yet a senior Iranian official is simultaneously telling Reuters that Iran will show no flexibility on enrichment or sending its highly enriched uranium stockpile abroad. That is not a minor difference.

I support diplomacy when diplomacy has something meaningful to accomplish. But negotiations require movement from both sides. Asking the United States to surrender significant military and economic leverage first, while declaring major nuclear issues nonnegotiable, is not much of an off-ramp. Hormuz remains closed. Military forces remain positioned throughout the region. The Houthis continue attacking Saudi Arabia. And Washington and Tehran remain very far apart on the issue that helped bring us here in the first place.

text:
Vicente Saldivar (left) and Sugar Ramos (right) battle for the World Featherweight Championship on September 26, 1964 in Mexico City with the defending titlist, Ramos, unable to answer the bell for the 13th round of his third defense.

The Associated Press reported that Saldivar "wore down the 24-year-old Ramos . . . and beat him to a bleeding pulp in the 10th and 11th rounds."
----------------------------------------------------------
From ESPN dot com on the passing of Sugar Ramos in 2017:

Former featherweight world champion Ultiminio "Sugar" Ramos, who was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2001, died on Sunday. He was 75.
The WBC, whose title was one that he held, announced the passing of Ramos, who boxed professionally from 1957 to 1972.
He was born in Cuba, turned pro at age 15 and fought there early in his career. But after the Communist revolution and the rise of dictator Fidel Castro, Ramos fled to Mexico, where he fought most of his career and lived in retirement.
On March 21, 1963, the 5-foot-4½ Ramos (55-7-4, 40 KOs), known for a powerful right hand, won the featherweight world title at age 21 at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles when he knocked out Davey Moore in the 10th round.
Sadly, however, the aftermath of that bout would long be remembered. Two days after the fight, Moore, whose head hit the bottom rope when he got knocked down and caused a severe brain stem injury, died. Moore was the second boxer to die from injuries in a fight with Ramos. In a 1958 fight in Cuba, Jose Blanco died after losing to Ramos by eighth-round knockout.
Ramos made three successful title defenses, defeating Raifu King by 15-round decision in Mexico City; Mitsunori Seki by sixth-round knockout in Japan; and Floyd Robertson by 15-round split decision, surviving a 13th-round knockdown in the process, in Ghana.
In September 1964, Ramos lost the 126-pound world title by 12th-round knockout to Vicente Saldivar in Mexico City.
Ramos notched five wins in a row following the defeat and was given a shot at lightweight world champion and fellow Hall of Famer Carlos Ortiz in October 1966. It was a highly controversial fight.
Ramos suffered a bad cut over his left eye, leading referee and Hall of Fame former light heavyweight champion Billy Conn to stop the fight and award Ortiz a fifth-round knockout victory. However, with the pro-Ortiz crowd of more than 30,000 going wild, the WBC eventually ordered a rematch and declared the title vacant, asserting that Conn was favoring Ortiz and that the fight should not have been stopped because of the cut.
They met again in July 1967, this time on Ortiz's home turf in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and Ortiz won by fourth-round knockout. It would be the final world title fight for Ramos, who fought nine more times, going 5-3-1.
"We will always remember Ultiminio as a great champion, but even more so, as a wonderful, friendly, genuine and kind man," WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman said in a statement. "A man of discerning style, always smart and elegant, often rakishly sporting a flamboyant hat, Ultiminio was adored by the people of his adopted country, certainly for his fighting spirit, but also for his unique character, chuckling sense of humor and his love of dancing and fun. He embraced the rhythm and the very essence of life.
"This is the saddest of losses, but the man with the big hands and the larger heart, leaves us with a wonderful legacy of joy and happiness."
----------------------------------------------------------
Vicente Saldivar, 37-3-0 with 26 KO wins, is a name that is forgotten by some but he was Mexico's first great Featherweight Champion well over a decade before the legendary Salvador Sanchez came along.

Born in one of the barrios on the outskirts of Mexico City, Vicente Saldivar at an early age would often get into fights both on the streets and in school, and developed a reputation around the area. Fearing that Vicente would head down the wrong path, his father decided to try to guide his energy into a sport where you could get recognition and praise for fighting: Boxing. So he took Vicente into a boxing gym where he would fall in love with the sport and became a successful amateur, winning the Mexican Golden Gloves as a Bantamweight. 
That victory would grant the 17-year-old Saldivar a spot on the Mexican Olympic team for the 1960 Olympics in Rome(The same Olympics where a young man named Cassius Clay would win a gold medal at Light Heavyweight). His Olympic dream wouldn't last long as he would be eliminated in the first round of the tournament against Ernst Chervet of Switzerland.
In his first few years as a pro, Saldivar built up a record of 16-0 (13 KOs) before he would suffer defeat at the hands of Cuba's Baby Luis via DQ in 1962. The following year he fixed the wrong by knocking out Luis in the 8th round of their rematch. He fought 3 more times that same year before, in 1964 he would get a chance to win the Mexican Featherweight title against Juan Ramirez, knocking him out in 2 rounds. He had defended the title once when he got an opportunity he couldn't refuse, a fight with the #1 ranked Featherweight at the time, Ismael Laguna of Panama, with the winner receiving a shot at the title.
By the time he faced Saldivar, Ismael Laguna's record was at 34-1 and he had already won the Panamanian Featherweight title. 
In the battle of the two Ffeatherweight prospects, Saldivar would take a 10 round decision and, with the victory, get his shot at the world title.
That same year, he would fight the then WBC and WBA Featherweight Champion, Cuban-Mexican Sugar Ramos.
The fight was at El Toreo de Cuatro Caminos in Mexico City and most experts chose Ramos to win the fight, believing Ultiminio's experience would ultimately win the day over Saldivar's raw aggression and power. 
However, in an epic and thrilling war between the two men fighting out of Mexico City, Saldivar surprised many by taking the initiative and wearing down the Cuban-Mexican with his vicious body attack. It was simply too much for Ramos, and after the 11th round, he retired on his stool. Vicente Saldivar was now the new WBA and WBC Featherweight Champion.
Saldivar would make seven title defenses, retiring after his third win over "The Welsh Wizard", Howard Winstone, in 1967.
----------------------------------------------------------
From boxrec:

Upon Vicente's retirement, the WBA & WBC declared the Featherweight Championship vacant and ordered their top contenders to fight for their respective titles. For the WBA, the top 2 contenders were Saldivar's former opponent Raul Rojas, & Enrique Higgins of Colombia. In the beginning, Rojas took the lead against Higgins with bulling, lunging tactics that broke the guard of the Colombian multiple times. But in the middle rounds, Enrique came back and started to put on a boxing clinic on Raul. By the 12th round, Rojas had multiple welts and mouses around his eyes and bleeding heavily by the nose. But just like Vicente, Raul persevered and in the 12th, he caught Higgins with a right hand, followed by a left and another right, and with that Enrique hit the canvas. he rose to his feet at the count of 8, came back out, and went toe-to-toe for the remainder of the round. For the next two rounds, Higgins attempted to regain what he had in the middle rounds, but it was gone and Rojas continued to batter him for the remainder of the fight. When the end came, it was almost too close to call, but in the end, it was a unanimous decision for Raul. And with that Raul Rojas was the new WBA Featherweight Champion...If only for a little while. A few months after he won the title, he would lose it in his first defense against Japan's Shozo Saijo. 
From then on, the WBA Featherweight title would transition to multiple legends such as Ernesto Marcel of Panama, Ruben Olivares, Nicaguragan Legend Alexis Arguello, Panama's Eusebio Pedroza & Barry McGuigan of Ireland.
Meanwhile, for the WBC, the top 2 contenders were none other than Saldivar's toughest opponents; Howard Winstone & Mitsunori Seki. For both men, it was their 4th attempt at trying to capture the Featherweight title, for Seki, it was his 5th attempt for a world title overall, and for Winstone, it was his first attempt at the title without Vicente there to defend it. With Saldivar watching among the crowd at the Royal Albert Hall in London, the Welshmen & the Japanese battled for the vacant WBC title. Both men put forth a gutsy effort, but Winstone was overall the better fighter, and he managed to cut Seki over his right eye. Upon being cut, the referee called a halt to bout to have look at the eye, which he decided was too dangerous to continue, and just like that, Howard Winstone was finally the Featherweight Champion of The World...But just like Raul Rojas, his reign wouldn't last long. After a non-title fight against BBBofC Super Featherweight Champion Jimmy Anderson, Howard would defend the title for the first time against a former opponent: Cuban-Spaniard, Jose Legra.
Known as "Pocket Cassius Clay" for having an uncanny resemblance to Ali, both physically and in his fighting style, and born in Baracoa, Cuba, Legra turned pro in 1960 and spent his first four years fighting in Cuba, Mexico, & Miami, Florida. When Fidel Castro slapped on the ban on professional boxing, Jose found himself in the same predicament that Sugar Ramos, Jose Napoles, and many other Cuban boxers found themselves in. But unlike other Cuban boxers who escaped to either Mexico or the U.S, Legra decided to go to Spain instead. That's where he went and that's where he stayed, gaining Spanish citizenship in 1966. from 1963 to 1965, Jose fought 27 times, winning 25 and drawing 2. That unbeaten streak was broken by none other than Howard Winstone, before his first fight with Saldivar. After the loss to Winstone, Legra would bounce back and go on a four year, 50 fight winning streak, winning the vacant EBU Featherweight title in the process. Then in 1968, he finally got his shot at the Featherweight title, as well as a chance at revenge as the WBC title was in the hands of Winstone. The effects of the fights with Vicente finally came out for Howard, as Jose knocked him down 2 times in the 1st round with looping overhand rights which also caused Winstone's left eye to swell quickly. For the next 4 rounds, Legra batter Howard from pillar to post, landing punches almost at will, and most of them hitting the swollen left eye. Then finally in the 5th round, with Jose landing multiple rights & Winstone almost completely helpless, referee Harry Gibbs decided enough was enough and mercifully stopped the fight. For Howard, it would be his last fight as he retired afterward, leaving a record of 61-6(27 KOs), and Legra, he was now the new WBC Featherweight Champion.
But it seemed as if the Featherweight Championship had some kind of curse on it. After two non-title fights in Spain & Paris, France, Jose decided to make his first defense of the title. For his 1st defense, he would head into neutral territory as he would take on a fighter he was fairly similar to him in terms of style and backstory; French-Australian, Johnny Famechon. Born as Jean-Pierre Famechon in Paris, France, Johnny was a highly skilled boxer whose greatest strength was his defense. He came from a prestigious boxing family. His father Andre Famechon was French Lightweight Champion, while his uncle Ray Famechon was French and EBU Featherweight Champion, and even challenged Willie Pep for the world Featherweight title in 1950, losing by unanimous decision. In 1948 Famechon's father and uncle Ray were offered to move to Australia and fight out of there. Andre took the offer and 2 years later brought the rest of his family over including Johnny. Once again, that's where he went & that's where he stayed. In 1961, with no amateur experience, Famechon decided to follow in his father and uncle's footsteps and made his professional debut, with his first bout ending up a draw. from 1961 to 1969, Johnny would build up a record of 47-4-6 (18 KOs), winning the Australian-Victorian State Featherweight title, the Australian Featherweight title, & the Commonwealth Featherweight title before getting his shot against Legra for the WBC title. In the battle between the talented dual nationality boxers, Famechon's defense carried him to victory as Jose couldn't find his range & got outboxed by the French-Australian.
With all the activity happening within the Featherweight division, Saldivar must've grown restless. Even though he had retired as Featherweight Champion, and with an almost perfect record, that wasn't enough for him. He wanted more, he was a born fighter and born fighters can he hear every second of every day tick by as they search for purpose again. Within the 2 years the Featherweight division lapsed into chaos, Saldivar assessed whether or not he still had the drive, the ability, and the hunger to still compete at the highest level of the sport. And in end, he concluded that he still had those things. And so on July 18th, 1969, Vicente returned to the ring. For his first comeback fight, Vicente decided to take a risk and face Jose Legra at the Inglewood Forum in Los Angeles, California.
At first, it seemed that the comeback would be a failure as Legra continuously tagged Saldivar with multiple right hands early rounds, and it seemed that it was all but confirmed when Jose floored him in the 3rd round with a right to the chin. But like always, Vicente persevered, he got up and in the 4th round, Saldivar returned to his old ways as he began hitting Legra's body with his ferocious body attack. It would prove to be the difference as Jose tired and Vicente grew stronger and sharper, tagging the Cuban-Spaniard with multiple left hands and staggering him in the 9th and 10th rounds. When the scorecards were read, it was a unanimous decision for the Mexican. It was official: Vicente Saldivar was back. 
Two weeks after Vicente's comeback win, Johnny Famechon made his first defense of the WBC Featherweight title. For his first defense, Johnny decided to have a homecoming bout as he would return to Australia against Fighting Harada of Japan.
Born as Masahiko Harada in Tokyo, Japan, Harada began his career as a Flyweight in 1960 and amassed a record of 26-1 with 10 KOs(Among his first opponents would be respected Japanese official Ken Morita & future Flyweight Champion Hiroyuki Ebihara) before receiving his first title shot in 1962 against Thailand legend Pone Kingpetch, knocking him out in the 11th round. His reign as Flyweight king wouldn't last long as Kingpetch would regain the title a year later, beating Masahiko by majority decision. Harada would then move up in weight, and in 1965 would become Bantamweight Champion, making 4 successful defenses before losing that title to another Australian, Lionel Rose. Masahiko decided to move up in weight again and go after the Featherweight title, the only thing standing between him and the championship was Famechon.
Their fight would be an intense one as Harada floored Johnny in rounds 2, 11, & 14, while Famechon would score his own down in round 4. At the end of the fight, Willie Pep, the referee and the only judge, initially declared the fight a draw, much to the dismay of Johnny's hometown crowd. It was then that Pep changed his scorecard, awarding Famechon the fight & allowing him to retain the title. Following a non-title victory over future Bantamweight Champion, Arnold Taylor, Famechon decided to give Masahiko another shot, going into Harada's hometown. This time Johnny would leave no doubts as he outboxed Masahiko, and in the 14th, knocked him out. It would be Harada's last fight as he would retire afterwards with a record of 55-7 (22 KOs).
With the threat of Fighting Harada gone, the stage was now set for Famechon vs Saldivar. The fight would in neutral territory as it would take place at the Palazzetto dello Sport in Roma, Italy. Vicente started strong, throwing his left hands and pounding away at Johnny's body while Famechon boxed from the outside and kept his jab constant. As the fight wore on, Saldivar started having trouble with Famechon who'd decided to pick up the pace, making Vicente miss with his defensive tactics and coming back with his own punches which caused Saldivar's right eye to swell, it was as if Vicente had entered the ring with Howard Winstone for the 4th time. In the 10th, Johnny turned up the tempo of his attack, targeting Saldivar's already swollen right eye. But Vicente, like he always had, persevered and in the 13th, he finally caught his man as Johnny's foot got tangled with Saldivar's, Vicente used the opportunity to land a left hook and with those combined forces, Famechon fell to the canvas. He took the mandatory-eight count, got up, & continued on. Once the referee waved him back in, Saldivar went straight at Johnny and fired away with shots, Famechon refused to back down and fired some of his own shots until the end of the round. The last two rounds mostly followed the same pattern; Vicente pressuring Johnny and firing away with body shots and left hands, while Famechon boxed from the outside throwing jabs to ward off Saldivar. With Vicente's early lead, Johnny's late rally, & the knockdown in the 13th, the fight was almost too close to call, but ultimately, the two judges, & the referee decided that Saldivar had done to warrant him the decision. With that, history was made in Italy when Vicente Saldivar became once again, the Featherweight Champion of the World. It would also be Johnny Famechon's last fight at he would retire afterwards at the age of only 25 with a record of 56-5-6(20 KOs).
But unlike last time, his reign wouldn't be long as 7 months later, he would make his first defense of his newly reclaimed title at the Auditorio Municipal in Tijuana against a relatively unknown Japanese fighter by the name of Kuniaki Shibata. Born in Hitachi, Japan, Shibata had turned pro in 1965 and built up a record of 23-1-1(15 KOs) before fighting for his first championship, the OPBF Featherweight title, against Hubert Kang of South Korea, losing by 6th-round KO. Kuniaki rebounded from the loss and won 6 fights before claiming the vacant Japanese Featherweight title against Yasuo Sakurai. He immediately vacated that title to pursue the world title, getting his first shot against Vicente. Shibata seized the opportunity for as soon as the bell rang to begin the fight, he came out of the corner, touched gloves with Saldivar, and went guns blazing, pitting Vicente in the neutral corner and firing away at his head and body. Saldivar got out of the corner and started box Kuniaki, firing jabs and his signature left hand, attempting to ward off the young, aggressive Japanese challenger. This was the pattern the first half of the fight followed; Shibata applying the pressure much like how Vicente used to while Saldivar himself used his boxing skills from the outside, and for a while, that pattern worked in Vicente's favor. But even though he had the lead, Kuniaki would not bend like Saldivar's previous opponents & Shibata gradually took control of the fight in the mid rounds, causing a cut on Saldivar's right cheek and punishing him heavily in the 10th. To Vicente's credit, he managed to come back and rally in the 11th, but even then, Shibata was still landing with jabs, right hands, & left hooks. Then in the 12th, Saldivar got caught with a straight right counter that hurt him. He managed to stay on his feet and finish the round, but it was clear that Vicente, cut underneath the right eye and also bleeding from the nose, was a beaten man, he was just not the same fighter he was back when he rallied to win against Howard Winstone or Mitsunori Seki; the only thing he had at this point was the heart and guts as he wanted to continue, but his trainer Adolfo Peres (Who had worked with former Bantamweight Champion, Raul Macias) wouldn't allow him to gain further punishment and didn't let him go out for 13th round. For the first time since Baby Luis all those years ago, and for the first time in a championship fight, Vicente Saldivar had lost, and now Kuniaki Shibata was the new WBC Featherweight Champion.
After the loss to Shibata, Saldivar stayed out of the ring for seven months, before returning in July of 1971 against contender and former world title challenger "Irish" Frankie Crawford. Born in Los Angeles (Other sources say Cleveland, Ohio), Crawford turned pro in 1965 and rose up the Featherweight rankings quickly, becoming a fan favorite in the city of angels where he fought often. He'd built up a record of 21-5-1 with 11 KOs before catching his big break when he was matched with up and coming Mexican-American Mando Ramos. Despite being outweighed by seven pounds(Frankie was just above the Featherweight limit at 127 lbs while Mando was just underneath the Lightweight limit at 134 lbs), Crawford put fourth a tremendous performance, opening up a cut over Ramos' left eye and keeping it a bloody mess en route a competitive majority decision victory. The two would have a rematch four months later, only this time Mando would have complete control of the fight, keeping Frankie at bay with his long jab and consistently landing with his right hand, winning the fight via unanimous decision.
Following the bouts with Ramos, Crawford would fight 15 times in 2 years (going 9-3-3 and winning the USA California State Featherweight title) before receiving another major break: A title shot against then WBA Featherweight Champion, Shozo Saijo. Initially, it looked as if Frankie would finally achieve his dream of becoming champion as he managed to drop Shozo with a left hook in the first round. To his credit, Saijo would get up and managed to stagger Crawford in the 9th and 10th rounds, the latter opening up a cut nearing Frankie's left ear. By the final round, both fighters were exhausted and clinched frequently. Crawford put fourth a tremendous effort, but in the end it was majority decision in favor of Shozo. Like with Mando Ramos, the two would have a rematch a year later. In a fight that was even closer than their first one, Saijo once again retained his title via unanimous decision. The bouts with Shozo would be the only time Crawford would fight for a world title. By the time Frankie faced Vicente at the Olympic Auditorium, he was on a 3 fight winning streak. In the beginning of the fight, Saldivar piled up an early lead by doing what had neglected to do against Kuniaki Shibata: Close the distance, cut off the ring, and bang the body of Frankie. The strategy worked well for the first 3 rounds and into the 4th round. Then seemingly out of nowhere, Crawford managed to get Vicente in the corner, and unleashed the same left hook that dropped Shozo Saijo. It didn't drop him, but the punch badly staggered Saldivar. Frankie, sensing an opportunity, slightly hesitated, then went in for the kill. But Saldivar, like he always had, preserved. Using all his experience, he managed to avoid the knockout blow and made it to the end of the round. Vicente regained his senses in between rounds, and in the 5th, he regained control of the fight,keeping it for the rest of the bout. When the bell rang to end the fight in the 10th round, Saldivar danced to his corner knowing he had scored a victory, and indeed he had, winning by unanimous decision.
The fight with Frankie Crawford, in all likelihood, should've been the final curtain call for Vicente and initially, it was as he retired again soon after. He had nothing left to prove or do in the sport of boxing; he had won the Featherweight title twice, he had beaten all the top names, and he had all but cemented his legacy as one of the best Featherweights of all time... But despite everything, he still craved to fight as he had almost his whole life; It was all he knew. So, three years after his last fight, he stepped into the ring once again for another shot at the world title.
In between his fight with Crawford and his second return to the ring, the Featherweight division was once again seeing frequent changes. 
Kuniaki Shibata, the man that beat Saldivar for the title, had made 2 defenses of the WBC crown (including a draw against future champion, Ernesto Marcel) before losing it to another Mexican named Clemente Sanchez by 3rd round knockout. After being stripped of the title for not making weight, Sanchez would lose to former champion Jose Legra, getting knocked down 11 times en route to a 10th round TKO, and making Legra a two-time champion. But just like his last reign, Jose's time at the top would be brief as he would lose the title to another former champion in the form of Brazil's Eder Jofre.

text:
In 2019, he officially created The Shaquille O'Neal Foundation to secure pathways and resources for underserved youth. Key initiatives include:

Shaq-a-Claus: An annual holiday tradition since 1997 that serves cities like Atlanta, Las Vegas, Orlando, and Compton. It has provided tens of thousands of toys, clothing, tech gadgets, and meals to underprivileged kids.

Shaq-to-School: A partnership with major brands to provide over $10 million worth of school supplies and backpacks to more than 5,000 Title-1 school kids nationally.

Comebaq Courts: Building and restoring community basketball courts and spaces in high-need neighborhoods to give kids a safe environment to play.

The Shaquille O'Neal Youth Development Complex: High-impact facilities currently being built in cities like Las Vegas and parts of Texas to offer athletic and academic spaces for youth.

School Grants: Committing hundreds of thousands of dollars in direct grants to funding-deprived Title-1 high schools.

text:
TRUMP'S FDA PICK CALLS MMR "SAFE AND EFFECTIVE," WEEKS AFTER STANDING BEHIND "QUITE LETHAL"

Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's nominee for commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration, sat before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee on Thursday, September 24, 2026, at 10:30 a.m. in 430 Dirksen. She is a physician (MD, University of New Mexico; PhD in clinical research, Johns Hopkins) and currently deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy. If confirmed she would replace Marty Makary, who resigned in May; Kyle Diamantas has been acting commissioner since then (ABC News, BioPharma Dive).

THE CONTRADICTION ON THE RECORD
On August 10, Trump signed Executive Order 14420, "Delivering Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations for Americans." Overton stood beside him in the Oval Office when, AP reports, he "falsely remarked" that the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal." The order says the MMR vaccine "should be administered in three separate single-disease shots once such products are domestically available," and gives HHS 90 days to present plans to offer core childhood vaccines as single shots, "starting with MMR," while "guaranteeing continued availability" of combination vaccines. In other words, the order itself concedes the separate shots are not available here now. Dr. Amesh Adalja of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security told ABC News the order "calls for splitting MMR into shots that don't exist," and that Overton's role "calls into question her scientific judgement."

WHAT SHE SAID THURSDAY
Chairman Bill Cassidy (R-La.), a physician, opened on exactly that: "You were standing behind President Trump when he called the MMR vaccine 'potentially quite lethal.' Is the MMR vaccine safe and effective?" (BioPharma Dive). Her answer, as Healio transcribed it: "The MMR vaccine is safe and effective ... The MMR vaccine is currently licensed and approved by the FDA. It is safe and effective, and it is our best tool right now in the public health response to the measles outbreak." Asked whether any vaccine on the market is unsafe, she said, per The Guardian and Roll Call: "Every vaccine on the U.S. market right now is safe and effective, according to the FDA." (ABC News renders it "are safe and effective.")

WHAT SHE DID NOT SAY
Cassidy said Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. "gave me guarantees, and he did not keep them," and asked what she would do if the president asked her to break hers. Overton said she would give the president her best advice and "follow the statutory requirements for the role of FDA commissioner regarding individual product determinations for safety and efficacy" (The Guardian). AP reports that later in the hearing she "declined to explicitly say that Trump was wrong about the MMR vaccine's safety." When Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) asked why she did not correct the president at the signing, she said the president was "providing additional options" (Healio).

MIFEPRISTONE
Overton, who wrote at the America First Policy Institute in 2023 that mail delivery of mifepristone was "dangerous to women," told Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) the drug "has met the safety and efficacy determinations of the FDA," and said she did not want to "prejudge" the FDA's ongoing safety review (AP). BioPharma Dive summarizes her pledge on vaccines and mifepristone as a promise to "follow the law."

THE VOTE MATH
The HELP roster lists 12 Republicans and 11 members caucusing with Democrats (10 Democrats plus Ranking Member Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.). A single Republican no would produce an 11 to 11 tie. Cassidy "didn't indicate whether he'd support Overton's nomination or when he might schedule a committee vote" (AP). Before the hearing he had called her role in the August order "almost disqualifying" (The Guardian). AP notes her abortion views could complicate winning over two Republicans who support federal abortion access, Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska. Senators had until 5 p.m. ET Friday, September 25, to submit written questions (Healio).

THE BACKDROP
CDC reports 3,659 confirmed U.S. measles cases in 2026 as of September 24, across 47 jurisdictions, with 40 new outbreaks, against 2,289 for all of 2025. CDC lists one 2026 measles death, a number it says is subject to change. The Guardian notes the count is the highest since 1991.

WHAT WE STILL DO NOT KNOW
Whether Cassidy will vote yes. When, or whether, a committee vote is scheduled. Whether Overton will be asked, in writing, the question she did not answer out loud. Her written testimony was not posted on the committee's hearing page as of Friday night. And what the HHS single-shot plan, due 90 days after August 10, will actually propose.

ZB30 is standing by on Capitol Hill.

text:
I think he wants to consolidate sub-par schools and have them offer more specialized education vs so much duplication of generalized courses.   Maybe that’s a bad idea, maybe it isn’t.  Doesn’t seem that outrageous. 

Conceptually year round school has always made a lot of sense to me.  
I would have chosen that for myself and for my kids were it available.  I prefer multiple 2 weeks breaks throughout the year vs one long 3 month break in the summer where a lot of boredom and learning loss tends to happen.   

That’s just my preference though and I assume would also be for some percentage of parents, especially working parents.  
 
It wouldn’t be the preference for many other kids and parents so I don’t think it should be mandated. But as far as I know he’s a huge proponent of school choice so it would be an option I assume.   

I’m not sure trying alternatives to improve kids education is the best example of why he’d be an awful governor but that’s just me.    

I’ve listened to him on multiple long form 2+ hour podcasts and I’ve found him eminently practical, thoughtful and competent.  

I see the criticism that he wants to turn all kids into ultra  high achievers, raise the bar x 100, spend 12 hours a day in school and studying.

That’s not for all kids or even most but given the incredibly low standards, low achievement and performance of our current system - where academic achievement is reserved for the few children who are naturally gifted, highly self motivated, connected and wealthy, erroring on side of raising the bar and being a little more the more rigorous and focused on quality education doesn’t seem like a horrible correction even if he’s a little extreme. 

That’s just how I see the issues you raised, but if those are the issues you vote on and you feel strongly his approach would be detrimental I understand why you wouldn’t vote for him.

Can I ask you- are you happy with the current state of education at the primary and university level in Ohio?  Are you achieving good outcomes with the current system?   
What are Ramaswamy’s opponents policies with regard to the issues you’ve raised or is education not one of her concerns?

text:
Below: The British Museum's collection of effigy pipes excavated from Mound City in Chillicothe, Ohio.
     Ephraim Squier & Dr. Edwin Davis dug out slightly over 200 effigy pipes from mounds at Mound City in 1846. A couple years later, the two early “archaeologists" had a dispute that had simmered for years. 
     Davis took most of the artifacts they had accumulated to New York. In 1851 Davis sought a buyer for all of his artifacts, which he claimed as his own. There were no American buyers who were interested nor was the Smithsonian interested. 
     In 1863 a British man named William Blackmore offered to buy them if no Americans would, but Blackmore wrote that they rightfully should stay in America. In 1864 Davis sold them to Blackmore for $10,000 (about $212,000 today).
      Blackmore had started a museum in Salisbury, England where they were displayed. In 1931 the Blackmore Museum sold them to the British Museum.

𝗬𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀

Spent some time crunching the numbers and exploring a different question:

How quickly does an offense turn possession into scoring?

Call it Productive Velocity, or PV10: touchdown-and-field-goal points produced per 10 minutes of possession.

Six points per offensive touchdown. Three per field goal. Exclude conversions, defensive scores, and return touchdowns.

Through September 19, 2026, using each team’s first four games:

𝗦𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗵 𝗗𝗮𝗸𝗼𝘁𝗮: 𝟭𝟯.𝟬𝟰
South Dakota State: 11.19
Youngstown State: 10.30
Montana State: 10.23

Here’s what caught my attention: all four teams run roughly 2.1 plays per possession minute. Yet the Coyotes produce more scoring value in that time.

And yes, USD’s numbers include Boise State.

This is an exploratory measure, not an official ranking or prediction. Opponents, field position, and clock strategy influence the results.

Still, it offers an encouraging perspective on this offense.

Having the ball is an opportunity. What you do with it is the story.

text:
50
A Psalm of Asaph.
1 The Mighty One, God, Jehovah, hath spoken,
And called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof.
2 Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty,
God hath shined forth.
3 Our God cometh, and doth not keep silence:
A fire devoureth before him,
And it is very tempestuous round about him.
4 He calleth to the heavens above,
And to the earth, that he may judge his people:
5 Gather my saints together unto me,
Those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.
6 And the heavens shall declare his righteousness;
For God is judge himself.
[Selah
7 Hear, O my people, and I will speak;
O Israel, and I will testify unto thee:
I am God, even thy God.
8 I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices;
And thy burnt-offerings are continually before me.
9 I will take no bullock out of thy house,
Nor he-goats out of thy folds.
10 For every beast of the forest is mine,
And the cattle upon a thousand hills.
11 I know all the birds of the mountains;
And the wild beasts of the field are mine.
12 If I were hungry, I would not tell thee;
For the world is mine, and the fulness thereof.
13 Will I eat the flesh of bulls,
Or drink the blood of goats?
14 Offer unto God the sacrifice of thanksgiving;
And pay thy vows unto the Most High;
15 And call upon me in the day of trouble:
I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me.
 
16 But unto the wicked God saith,
What hast thou to do to declare my statutes,
And that thou hast taken my covenant in thy mouth,
17 Seeing that thou hatest instruction,
And castest my words behind thee?
18 When thou sawest a thief, thou consentedst with him,
And hast been partaker with adulterers.
19 Thou givest thy mouth to evil,
And thy tongue frameth deceit.
20 Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother;
Thou slanderest thine own mother’s son.
21 These things hast thou done, and I kept silence;
Thou thoughtest that I was altogether such a one as thyself:
But I will reprove thee, and set them in order before thine eyes.
 
22 Now consider this, ye that forget God,
Lest I tear you in pieces, and there be none to deliver:
23 Whoso offereth the sacrifice of thanksgiving glorifieth me;
And to him that ordereth his way aright
Will I show the salvation of God.

text:
Jamal Rule is from Salisbury, North Carolina. Three-star recruit. The only schools that offered him were Nebraska, Michigan State, Syracuse and Virginia Tech.

He's also one of the fastest big men you'll find. At Charlotte Christian he won the state title in the indoor 500 meters at 1:04.07, which was the ninth fastest time in the entire country that season.

He weighs 210 pounds.

On his recruiting profile, in the section where most kids list their bench press, he wrote this instead.

"Each time I step on the field, I remind myself that playing football is an honor that many players never receive. I watched my parents make countless sacrifices which drives me to make the most of every opportunity life presents."

September 5, his first college game. Nebraska vs Ohio at Memorial Stadium.

Dana Holgorsen said that when Rule showed up in the summer, he was a nervous, anxious kid walking around campus with wide eyes.

Mekhi Nelson, the junior running back, could hear him through the wall before kickoff, hyping himself up so loud that Nelson had to tell him to save some of it for the game.

Then the team walked to the mouth of the tunnel and Rule saw the crowd.

"Just walking out onto the field seeing all the fans, I teared up a little bit. I was like, wow. It's great to be here."

He got the ball three straight times inside the red zone on Nebraska's first drive and scored on the third.

By the end of the day he had 122 rushing yards, 47 receiving, and three touchdowns on 17 touches.

He became the first Nebraska freshman running back to run for 100 yards in a season opener since 2004, and just the sixth Big Ten freshman since 1995 with two rushing touchdowns and a receiving touchdown in the same game. PFF graded him the second best running back in the country that week.

Here's the part that tells you who he is.

Late in the game, with Nebraska up big, Memorial Stadium started chanting.

RUUUUUUULE.

He didn't think it was for him. Nebraska has a tight end named Luke Lindenmeyer who gets a chant that sounds almost identical, and Rule assumed that's who they meant.

Then it happened again.

"Whoa. That's me."

He's now the third leading rusher in the Big Ten. Holgorsen was asked this week whether they'd scale him back.

"He doesn't look like a freshman to me, so we won't treat him like one."

text:
The Journey of Forgiveness and Confession:

Healing the Soul

We were shown our righteous sins (Instances of: “I have been sinned against in this way, I hate that sinner, and I have no mercy for them!”). We were encouraged to forgive without the trespasser’s confession or request for forgiveness.

We forgave those who had severely wronged us. We pulled those unrighteous spears from our soul and our wounds healed.

We worked our way up through our life, our soul forgiving all trespassers. Forgiveness of sin was for our benefit, not for those who had trespassed against us. Our forgiveness was healing us!

We were then shown our trespasses. We asked GOD for forgiveness but the thorns were not removed. We were allowed to experience the pain we had caused others, and we cried tears of remorse!

We were overcome with love and remorse and decided to take the leap of faith and confess. We opened the front door to our house (no confession and no temperance) and hesitated for a moment, tears running down our face as we gathered our courage.

Our sins weighed heavier on some of those we sinned against, affecting their lives more than they did others. When we were forgiven, others were healed. Remorse and confession healed us. It was necessary to be completely truthful when confessing our sins and we described them to the best of our ability. Does not the memory of a heavy burden weigh more than a lesser burden?

During and after our confessional baptism we felt an agony of remorse. This required faith to endure. Remorse was the process of sin leaving our soul and cleansing us. The spirit of truth testified to the validity of “Confessional Baptism.” The weights of our burdens lifted and there was rejoicing on all sides! We were all being made anew! We tackled the hardest confessions first, and it was easier as we went along.

We listened to GOD by tapping the gold mine within us. We went where GOD told us to go —to our confessions. Only after our sins were unearthed and refined by fire (Confessional Baptism) were they worth their weight in GOLD—GOD. HEAVENLY CURRENCY was created and prayers, Prayers and PRAYERS were answered, Answered and ANSWERED! We were having fellowship with one another; we walked in the light and we loved the LIGHT!

Now the memory of a wrong did not vanish. The weights of our wrongs vanished. It was the sin that no longer had weight and the memory of salvation superseded it!

Humbleness, mercy and guidance were the yield and our return to temperance, Temperance and TEMPERANCE was the answered prayer, Prayer and PRAYER.

1st Forgiveness for all, confessional baptism, and our return to temperance amended the environment around us.

2nd The environment had been primed and our armor had been tempered. We left our “home town” prepared to Forgive All Sin, Confess All Sin and Practice All Temperance. Against such things there was no commandment.

3rd We went into the desert for forty days and forty nights (Forgiving All, Confessing to All and Practicing All Temperance). The sins within others became as clear as day in the absence of all sin within us and we were tested. Those whom we loved offered us power and wealth and all that is sinful in return: stones to eat instead of bread, and poison to drink instead of water. Our refusal caused offense. Tables overturned within every temple and unhealthy offerings tumbled to the ground just as coins once did. Those whom we loved turned against us (no love). We fasted. In that desert we were alone for forty days and forty nights.

Only after forgiveness for all and confessional baptism did the “clean spirit” enter, and we were born, again (I am, I am who I am). We ate and we drank and we were merry (forgiven all and confessed to all). A New Year’s Resolution (temperance) followed. One holy spirit at a time this dimly lit world Brightened. MERRY CHRISTMAS!

The New Testament: Heaven is a Full-Time Job; Blessed are those who return to temperance through Christ!

Since this silly robot is ignoring my tag, I went and asked it directly: 

Yes. Archaeology and extra-biblical inscriptions have confirmed the existence of numerous people, places, and events mentioned in the Bible that some 19th- and 20th-century scholars treated as legendary, late inventions, or historically unreliable. Confirmation of a name or site does not prove every detail of the surrounding narrative or theological claims, and debates continue over scale, dating, and interpretation (especially for the Patriarchs, Exodus, Conquest, and the size of the United Monarchy). Still, the list of once-doubted items that later received independent attestation is substantial.

People
King David: Some scholars viewed David as a late literary or legendary figure, or at most a minor local chieftain. The Tel Dan Stele (discovered 1993–94), an Aramaic victory inscription from the 9th century BCE, refers to the “House of David” (bytdwd). Most scholars accept this as the earliest extra-biblical reference to David’s dynasty. Possible additional references appear on the Mesha Stele and in Shishak’s Karnak inscription.

Belshazzar: Daniel 5 presents him as the last ruler of Babylon, offering Daniel the position of “third ruler.” Extra-biblical sources listed Nabonidus as the final king and omitted Belshazzar, leading critics to treat him as a biblical invention. Clay cylinders from Ur (1854) and other inscriptions name Belshazzar as Nabonidus’s eldest son and co-regent who governed Babylon while his father was away. This explains why he could only offer the third-highest rank.

Sargon II of Assyria: Isaiah 20:1 is the only ancient reference to this king for a long time; commentators often assumed it was an alternate name for another known Assyrian ruler. Paul-Émile Botta excavated Sargon’s palace at Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad) in 1843, confirming both the king and his campaign against Ashdod.

Pontius Pilate: Known from the Gospels, Josephus, Philo, and Tacitus, but no contemporary inscription existed until the Pilate Stone was found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961. It names “[Pon]tius Pilatus, [Praef]ectus Iuda[ea]e.”

Joseph Caiaphas: The high priest who appears in the Gospels. A decorated ossuary discovered in a Jerusalem tomb in 1990 is inscribed “Yehosef bar Qayafa” (“Joseph son of Caiaphas”). A second ossuary mentioning a granddaughter of Caiaphas was later authenticated. Most scholars accept that the tomb belongs to the Caiaphas priestly family; many consider the ornate box likely that of the high priest himself.

Lawrence Mykytiuk of Purdue has catalogued 53 figures from the Hebrew Bible (plus additional New Testament figures) attested in inscriptions from the relevant period. These include Egyptian pharaohs (Shishak/Sheshonq I, Necho II, Taharqa), Israelite and Judahite kings (Omri, Ahab, Jehu, Hezekiah, Jehoiachin), and officials such as Tattenai and Sanballat.

The Hittites are a related case: they were long known only from the Bible and widely dismissed as fictional. Excavations at Hattusa (Boğazköy) from the late 19th century onward revealed a major Late Bronze Age empire. Debate continues over whether every biblical use of “Hittite” refers to the Anatolian empire or to related Neo-Hittite groups and local Canaanite populations.

Places
Nineveh: After its destruction in 612 BCE the city’s precise location was forgotten; classical writers and later observers sometimes treated its grandeur as legendary. Mid-19th-century excavations by Austen Henry Layard and others at Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus identified the site opposite Mosul and recovered Sennacherib’s palace and Ashurbanipal’s library.

Pool of Siloam: Mentioned in John 9 as the site of Jesus’ healing of a blind man and in the Old Testament in connection with Hezekiah’s water works. Its exact Second Temple-period location was uncertain until 2004, when a large stepped pool matching the period was uncovered during sewer work in the City of David.

Hezekiah’s Tunnel (Siloam Tunnel): The Bible describes Hezekiah diverting the Gihon Spring to protect Jerusalem’s water supply (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32). The tunnel itself and the Siloam Inscription (found 1880) describing its construction corroborate the account. Recent work has also identified an earlier dam that formed the pool.

Other confirmed or strongly supported sites include the City of David excavations, the Pool of Bethesda, and numerous towns listed in the biblical conquest and monarchic narratives.

Events
Sennacherib’s 701 BCE campaign against Judah: The Bible describes the Assyrian invasion, capture of many cities, and failed siege of Jerusalem. Sennacherib’s own prism (Taylor Prism and others) records the same campaign, lists 46 fortified cities taken, and describes shutting Hezekiah “like a bird in a cage” in Jerusalem—matching the biblical outline while omitting any miraculous deliverance.

Fall of Jerusalem and Babylonian exile: Extra-biblical Babylonian records (including ration tablets naming King Jehoiachin) and the destruction layers in Jerusalem align with 2 Kings and Jeremiah.

Shishak/Sheshonq I’s campaign: 1 Kings 14 and 2 Chronicles 12 describe an Egyptian invasion of Judah. Sheshonq’s Karnak relief lists conquered towns in the region.

The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) provides the earliest extra-biblical mention of “Israel” as a people already in Canaan.

These discoveries shifted the burden of proof for many specific names and sites. They do not settle larger questions about the composition of the biblical texts or the historicity of unattested early events, but they demonstrate that a substantial portion of the Bible’s historical framework rests on real people, places, and political events that were independently recorded by Israel’s neighbors.

27
A Psalm of David.
1 Jehovah is my light and my salvation;
Whom shall I fear?
Jehovah is the strength of my life;
Of whom shall I be afraid?
2 When evil-doers came upon me to eat up my flesh,
Even mine adversaries and my foes, they stumbled and fell.
3 Though a host should encamp against me,
My heart shall not fear:
Though war should rise against me,
Even then will I be confident.
4 One thing have I asked of Jehovah, that will I seek after:
That I may dwell in the house of Jehovah all the days of my life,
To behold the beauty of Jehovah,
And to inquire in his temple.
5 For in the day of trouble he will keep me secretly in his pavilion:
In the covert of his tabernacle will he hide me;
He will lift me up upon a rock.
6 And now shall my head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me;
And I will offer in his tabernacle sacrifices of joy;
I will sing, yea, I will sing praises unto Jehovah.
 
7 Hear, O Jehovah, when I cry with my voice:
Have mercy also upon me, and answer me.
8 When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee,
Thy face, Jehovah, will I seek.
9 Hide not thy face from me;
Put not thy servant away in anger:
Thou hast been my help;
Cast me not off, neither forsake me, O God of my salvation.
10 When my father and my mother forsake me,
Then Jehovah will take me up.
11 Teach me thy way, O Jehovah;
And lead me in a plain path,
Because of mine enemies.
12 Deliver me not over unto the will of mine adversaries:
For false witnesses are risen up against me,
And such as breathe out cruelty.
13 I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of Jehovah
In the land of the living.
14 Wait for Jehovah:
Be strong, and let thy heart take courage;
Yea, wait thou for Jehovah.

text:
Cassandra was one of the most tragic figures in Greek Mythology. She was daughter of Priam of Troy (therfore sister of Hector and Paris). She was so beautiful that Apollo offer her the gift of prophecy. However she died the God's love, so Apollo transformed her gift to tell the future but without anyone believing her.

She tried to warn Priam, Hector and Trojans several times :

Cassandra predicted destruction of Troy when Paris was born to Hecabe. Cassandra’s first commonly told prediction again involves Paris, but from years later, when her brother returns to Troy with Helena. Hector would chastise his brother for his actions, but Cassandra told how she now saw the future ruin of Troy, but of course, as per the curse of Apollo, Cassandra was ignored.
 
The abduction of Helen would of course lead to Trojan War and during war Cassandra would witness many of her brothers die in defence of Troy. Eventually, Achaeans came up with a plan to finally take the city of Troy, and a Wooden Horse was constructed, and then seemingly abandoned outside the city walls. Cassandra immediately saw what would happen if Trojans were to take possession of horse and whilst Cassandra tried to convince her kinsmen of risk, she was of course ignored. Thus, Wooden Horse, with its belly full of Achaean heroes, was taken into Troy, leading, that night, to Sacking of Troy.

During the sack of the city, Cassandra was found by Ajax the Lesser hiding in Athena's temple, he dragged Cassandra from the altar of Athena and raped her. Athena, furious, killed Ajax with a blow. The rape of Cassandra by Ajax was a favourite scene in Greek art. However, the fate of Cassandra got worse, as Achaeans disputed who would take her as trophy with Agamemnon eventually got her as concubine. In the end, in the palace of Mycenes, Cassandra was violently murdered by Agamemnon's jealous wife, Clytemnestra.

📷 : Timeless Tale of Tragedy and Triumph - "Ajax and Cassandra" by Solomon Joseph Solomon (1886) -

Whoever saw Solomon Joseph Solomon's masterpiece, "Ajax and Cassandra" (1886), immediately struck by the sheer intensity and emotion that radiated from the canvas. This monumental work of art, measuring an impressive 7ft by 10ft, captures a pivotal moment in Greek mythology, where the Trojan princess Cassandra is forcibly taken from sanctuary of Athena by Greek hero Ajax the Lesser.

Solomon's masterful use of color and light breathes life into this tragic scene. The rich, deep hues of the temple's interior contrast with the golden glow of the setting sun, casting an ethereal light upon the figures. This juxtaposition of darkness and light serves to heighten the drama and tension of the moment, as the viewer is drawn into the struggle between the two central characters.

The artist's attention to detail is nothing short of extraordinary. The intricate patterns on the temple's columns and the delicate folds of the characters' garments showcase Solomon's skill and dedication to his craft. The expressions on the faces of the onlookers, ranging from horror to disbelief, further emphasize the gravity of the situation.

At the heart of the painting, we find the ill-fated Cassandra, her eyes filled with terror and despair as she clings to the statue of Athena. Her vulnerability is palpable, and one cannot help but feel a deep sense of empathy for her plight. Ajax, on the other hand, is depicted as a powerful and imposing figure, his muscular form and determined expression embodying the ruthless nature of war.

What truly sets "Ajax and Cassandra" apart, however, is way in which Solomon manages to convey timeless themes of tragedy and triumph. The painting serves as a poignant reminder of human cost of war and devastating consequences of unchecked ambition. At same time, it celebrates the resilience of the human spirit, as Cassandra's defiance in the face of adversity continues to inspire viewers more than a century after painting's creation.
