text:
The man who wrote Black Americans back into their own country's history wrote much of it from a room barely bigger than a closet, because the state archive would not let him sit with the white researchers. His name was John Hope Franklin, and he would end his life holding the Presidential Medal of Freedom and more than a hundred honorary degrees.

They got to decide where he was allowed to sit. He got to decide what the entire country would one day have to admit about itself, so think hard about the kind of nerve that took.

The state of Alabama handed him the records he asked for, then told him there was nowhere in the building he was allowed to sit.

He stood in the middle of the floor holding the documents. White researchers sat at the tables around him. He looked for a corner where no one was sitting, so that no one could accuse him of putting himself where he did not belong.

He started toward it. The attendant, an older white woman, told him he could not sit there either.

So they found him a room. It was slightly larger than a closet, with a table, a chair, and a wastebasket, and that is where John Hope Franklin worked for the better part of a year.

That closet is where the history got written.

He was gathering the proof, in the country's own handwriting, that Black people had been part of the American story from the very beginning. He was doing it from a closet because the reading room was reserved for whites.

He did not raise his voice about it. He took the room, and he took the documents into the room, and he got to work.

He had learned young that the truth cost something, because he had watched his own father pay for it.

Buck Colbert Franklin was the son of a man born into slavery, and one of the first Black lawyers in Oklahoma. In the spring of 1921 he kept a law office in the Greenwood district of Tulsa.

Greenwood was thirty-five square blocks of Black-owned banks, hotels, theaters, and shops. People across the country knew it by another name, and that name was Black Wall Street.

On the night of May 31, 1921, a white mob set out to destroy it, and did.

It began the way so many of these things began, with a crowd gathering to lynch a young Black man over an accusation that fell apart almost as fast as it spread. By the next morning Greenwood was burning.

More than a thousand homes were gone. Franklin's father, watching from the street, described airplanes passing overhead and dropping burning turpentine down onto the rooftops.

The city's official records counted thirty-six dead. Historians who have spent careers on it since believe the real number may have been closer to three hundred.

Buck Franklin's office burned with everything else on the block.

What he did next is the reason there was still a Greenwood left to remember at all. Five days after the massacre, there is a photograph of him back at work, seated in a Red Cross tent with his law partner beside him and their secretary taking down notes.

The city had rushed through a fire ordinance built to keep Black families from rebuilding on their own land. Franklin carried the fight all the way to the Oklahoma Supreme Court, and he beat it.

Greenwood rose a second time out of its own ashes. By 1925 the shops had reopened.

A decade after the smoke cleared, Buck Franklin sat down and wrote ten pages describing exactly what he had seen. Then he folded the pages and put them away.

That account stayed lost until 2015, when it turned up in a storage room and was given to the Smithsonian. For most of the century in between, you could read an American history textbook cover to cover and never learn that Tulsa had happened.

His son was six years old the summer the city burned.

John Hope Franklin was waiting in a small Oklahoma town with his mother, expecting any day to join his father in Tulsa. The massacre kept the family apart for more than four years.

He wrote later that a race riot had split his family before he was old enough to understand what a race riot even was. He already understood the smaller version of it, though.

That same year, a train conductor put him and his mother off the train during a six-mile trip, because she had refused to move to the car set aside for Black passengers. She would not let her son cry about it.

He carried all of it into a life's work.

He went to Fisk University, and then to Harvard, where he became the first student from a Black college admitted into the graduate history program with no conditions attached. He finished his doctorate in 1941.

Then he set out to do the thing almost no white university in the country wanted done. He would put Black Americans back into the history of the nation, and he would prove every word of it using the nation's own documents.

That is what sent him into the segregated archives in the first place. He gave himself a course in a history no school had ever taught him, and then went hunting for the evidence in libraries built to keep him out.

At Duke University, he was permitted to read the rare manuscripts and forbidden from using the restroom. He did not forget it, and years later that same university would come asking him to join its faculty as one of the most decorated professors it ever had.

In 1947 the book arrived. It was called From Slavery to Freedom, and it has since sold more than three and a half million copies and never once gone out of print.

Before it, the serious study of Black history barely existed inside the academy. After it, the old habit of writing Black people out of the American story became a much harder lie to tell.

He did more than write the history down. In 1956 he became the first Black scholar to chair a history department at a mostly white university, and in 1965 he walked the road from Selma to Montgomery with everyone else who had decided that walking was now part of the work too.

Then the phone rang, and it was Thurgood Marshall.

Marshall was building the case against segregated schools, and he needed a historian who could tell the Supreme Court what the men who wrote the Fourteenth Amendment had actually meant to do about segregation. He did not phrase it as a request.

Franklin remembered the offer as something closer to a threat, that if he did not agree to work for Marshall, then Marshall pitied what was going to happen to him.

So Franklin spent his days buried in Reconstruction records, assembling the history underneath the argument. In 1954, in Brown v. Board of Education, the Court struck segregation in public schools down.

He believed, at first, that the country would simply follow its own highest law. He did not yet know that other men were already sitting up through the night, working out how to get around the ruling before the ink had dried.

By the time he was eighty, he had gathered more than a hundred honorary degrees and nearly every honor his profession could offer.

In the fall of 1995 he was in Washington to accept the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor this country gives a citizen. The evening before the ceremony, he was having dinner at the Cosmos Club, where he had been a member for years.

A white woman crossed the room, handed him her coat check, and told him to go bring her coat.

He was eighty years old, the most honored historian in America, one day from the Medal of Freedom, and a stranger had looked at all of it and seen a servant. He once answered a man who waved such stories away by writing that a life of privilege had likely spared him from ever having to know what a Black person meets on any ordinary day, whatever his age or his station.

At home in Durham he kept a greenhouse full of orchids. There were more than a hundred of them, slow and stubborn flowers that give nothing back to anyone in a hurry.

He tended them the way he had tended the record of his country. Slowly, and without ever deciding it was hopeless.

He never dressed up what he found in the archives, and he never pretended that finding it had been a neutral act. "We've got to tell the unvarnished truth," he said.

Near the end of his life he said it another way. "We have to confront history," he told an interviewer at ninety. "We have to face it down to be certain that it won't haunt us again."

He did not live to see the answer. He died in 2009, at ninety-four.

The people who remember Tulsa with their own eyes are almost all gone now. In November of 2025, Viola Fletcher died at the age of a hundred and eleven, still waiting for the justice she had once asked Congress for to its face.

Four years before that, she had sat in front of lawmakers and told them what she still carried. She said she could still see the shooting, still smell the smoke, still hear the airplanes overhead.

She had also told them that the city of Tulsa used the victims' names and the images of their suffering to draw money into the city, while the people it happened to got nothing.

She died without a single dollar of it ever set right. The year before, the Oklahoma Supreme Court had thrown out the survivors' lawsuit, agreeing that their grievance was real and legitimate, and ruling that the law simply had nothing to offer them.

As these words are written, one survivor is still living. Lessie Benningfield Randle turned a hundred and eleven in November, and she has spent her last years asking this country not to look away, and not to let what happened be quietly lifted out of its schoolbooks.

Franklin spent sixty years building a record so complete that this could never again be denied. The denial did not end. It only changed its clothes, from the archive that would not give him a chair to the people now arguing that children should be spared the trouble of learning any of it.

He wrote the truth from a room the size of a closet, the same way his father wrote it from a borrowed tent. Neither man was ever going to be able to hold that door open by himself.

That part was always going to come down to whoever stood in the room after him. The record is finished, and the record is true.

Whether it stays read is the only thing still undecided, and that part belongs to us.

text:
🚨WOW!!!

An 81-year-old man was hauling heavy suitcases up a flight of stairs, 14 HOURS A DAY, to pay for his wife's CANCER TREATMENT...

...then the woman at the top of those stairs opened her door, heard his story, and raised him $600,000 to GO HOME to be with his wife!!!! ❤️

His name is Don Johnson.

He's 81 years old, from The Colony, Texas, just outside Dallas.

His wife Josephine has been by his side for 57 YEARS. She's fighting an aggressive cancer.

Three years ago, when the medical bills started piling up, Don went looking for work.

He tried Amazon. He tried Walmart. Nobody would take him.

So he became an independent contractor delivering lost airline luggage to people's front doors.

Sometimes 14 hours a day. Hundreds of miles in a single shift. Driving as far as OKLAHOMA to get a bag to its owner.

He put over 200,000 MILES on his own car doing it.

At 81 years old.

"I appreciate what we do get from insurance, but it doesn't cover it all. And cancer treatment is very expensive."

Then on a September day he dropped a suitcase on the steps outside a home in The Colony.

A woman named Erin Howell heard the noise on her door cam and came outside.

She offered to help carry it, and she asked him a simple question: why is a man your age doing this?

His answer: "It's the only job that will hire me."

Then he told her about Josephine.

Erin could have wished him well and gone back inside.

Instead she started a GoFundMe and a TikTok page called "Help Don Retire."

She wrote that at an age when he should be resting by his wife's side, he was out on the highway lifting bags to keep her alive.

The goal was $150,000.

It blew past that in DAYS.

Then $281,000.
Then $370,000.
Now more than $600,000 and still climbing.

More than ELEVEN THOUSAND people gave.

But here's the part that got me...

Right before all of this, Don's car had started breaking down and he'd already been forced to cut back his hours.

He was running out of road.

And that's exactly when a stranger he'd talked to for five minutes knocked on the whole country's door and AMERICA showed up.

"I left and thought I'd never see her again," Don said. "And it was an amazing thing she did for me, for us."

His wife, Josephine says after 57 years, she's watching "for better or worse" happen right in front of her.

"I'm so happy that he turned out to be the man he is."

And Don? He's not talking about himself.

"I love her dearly, and I just want her to be well. It restores my faith in people. For her and others to do for me, that was a miracle. I look forward to the day that I can help people just like I'm being helped now."

He never asked for a dime.
He just kept carrying the bags.

GOD BLESS Don and Josephine Johnson, and GOD BLESS Erin Howell.

THIS IS THE AMERICA I KNOW!!! 🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸

text:
Ugly Duck Labs: a failed project, by the numbers 🦆📉

Launched in Feb 2025 with 1,851 ducks. Almost 20 months later:

Total volume: about $4,186. That's the entire lifetime trading of the collection. Many projects do more in one afternoon.
Floor: about $37 (0.014 ETH), down 8.5% in a single day.
Top offer: about $22. Buyers won't even pay the floor. They're bidding 40% under it.
Only 213 unique owners for 1,851 NFTs. That's 11.5%. Nearly 9 out of 10 ducks are sitting in a small number of wallets. There's no community, just a pile of unsold inventory.
Price is falling apart. A duck that once sold for $161 is now listed at $51.
7% creator fee on a collection nobody's trading. Charging a premium tax on a dead market.

So what's the fix? Airdrop them for free. When you can't sell them, you give them away and call it a reward.

Scrooge told me giving ducks away was something I'd regret. Now he's doing exactly that, just because nobody's buying. 🍬

text:
Happy Birthday George Raft

The fascinating, but bone-headed George Raft is most frequently identified with his suave portrayals of gangsters in the 1930s and 40s, but he was also an erotic dancer, and in later life, a potential comedian. Raft was born in New York City in 1895. His mother taught him how to dance, and he began performing exhibition dances before working in nightclubs, where he took things up a notch. “I could have been the first X-rated dancer," he boasted later. "I was very erotic. I used to caress myself as I danced. I was never a Fred Astaire or a Kelly, but I was sensuous”. Raft helped popularise the tango and the Charleston in Paris, London and New York. Fred Astaire, in his autobiography “Steps in Time”, wrote that Raft did "the fastest Charleston I ever saw." During this time, he foolishly befriended a number of gangsters. A boyhood acquaintance of "Bugsy" Siegel, and later a "wheel man" for the mob, Raft acknowledged having narrowly avoided a life of crime. His screen debut was in the lost “Queen of the Night Clubs” starring Texas Guinan, and he followed this with a part in “Gold Diggers of Broadway.” His dancing skills were noticed by director Rowland Brown, who cast him as Spencer Tracy's sidekick in “Quick Millions” (1931), which led to a contract with Paramount. Raft said he never regarded himself as an actor: “I wanted to be me.” His big break came when he played the second lead in Howard Hawks's “Scarface”. Raft's performance was notable for his character's habit of flipping a coin, which became an iconic trope in gangster films. He was correct when he said he wasn’t an actor, but he had animal magnetism on the screen. When “Scarface” was released, the public response was so enthusiastic that Raft was offered the lead in “Night After Night” (1932). He then starred in “Bolero” (1934), playing a dancer opposite Carole Lombard. In May, the actor signed a new contract with Paramount to reflect his star status. He appeared in Dashiell Hammett's “The Glass Key” (1935) and in 1937 was the third highest-paid star in Hollywood. The actor received an offer from Warner Bros. to appear opposite James Cagney in the prison drama “Each Dawn I Die” (1939); the movie was a considerable success and Warners offered Raft a contract. Hal Wallis later wrote that "Our association with Raft was a constant struggle from start to finish. Hypersensitive to public accusations of underworld connections, he flatly refused to play the heavy in any film... Time and time again we offered him gangster parts and time and time again he turned them down." In Raoul Walsh's trucking melodrama “They Drive by Night” (1940), Raft played the lead, co-starring with Ann Sheridan and Humphrey Bogart. He stupidly declined “High Sierra” and “The Maltese Falcon” (1941), and both roles were played by Bogie, catapulting the latter to stardom. Raft instead made “Manpower” (1941), with Edward G. Robinson and Marlene Dietrich. Robinson recalled Raft as "touchy, difficult and thoroughly impossible to play with." During filming, Raft and Robinson came to blows, with photographs of the brawl splashed across newspapers. Raft went freelance, and immediately refused the lead in “Double Indemnity.” Director Billy Wilder later said, "We knew then that we'd have a good picture". He next appeared in the popular “Whistle Stop” (1946) with newcomer Ava Gardner. The actor followed this with a series of thrillers; none performed strongly at the box office. His career was effectively dead, but In 1958, Raft was offered a role in “Some Like It Hot” (1959), sending up his own performances as a gangster. He was surprisingly funny and appeared as a casino owner in the Rat Pack movie” Ocean's 11”. In his final years, Raft was beset by illness and legal problems, which included federal claims for unpaid taxes. George Raft died from emphysema at the age of 79, on November 24, 1980. Had his brains not been in his erotic dancing, he might be better remembered today.

text:
This is a @garyvee appreciation post. 

I’ve worked remotely, in sales, for a very long time. My job is emotionally demanding and challenging, in a competitive market. One day, 8 years ago, I found one of Gary’s videos and loved his energy.  I loved that he expressed himself so directly and passionately and I thought, finally, someone I can relate to…. 

And his content came at a really interesting time in my life… 

I had been dealing with toxic friendships, working through unhealthy perspectives, judging people too harshly and yet, truly believed I was being the better person because “I love people”.  I couldn’t properly balance ego/competition vs empathy/understanding/transparency.  Looking back, I connected with Gary’s “direct” energy. I just didn’t know how to communicate it well in my own life. I’m sure my childhood played a role, but that’s a whole other story I won’t get into. :) 

For those on the outside, it had to be easy to see, but those close to me were too kind to tell me the truth. Perhaps they knew my intentions and could see I meant well. But, change had to happen, eventually. 

The Covid era exposed a lot of different personalities. It felt like everyone was coming to social media to express opinions. There was so much panic, confusion and worldwide divide — everything felt so zoomed in.  It was a time to truly learn more about others and ourselves in a way we hadn’t experienced before on such levels.  It exposed so much. It was a window of opportunity.  

During that time, Gary started a show, Tea with Garyvee, to chat with people and offer advice and value to the guest and listeners.  It was that year when I started to wake up, and truly look within myself and realize what needed to change.  Gary is responsible for this. 

I became super involved with the community and looked forward to the guests on Marketing for the Now, taking notes, connecting with other leaders… I just wanted to keep learning, and consuming… and improving myself. 

I’ve spent almost every day since then learning from Gary, and others in the VeeFriends community.  Constantly evolving, growing, watching…. So much time….. seeing how praise/criticism is handled. That time was/is invaluable to me.  

I really wanted to share this in hopes that people would understand the depths of what Gary has gone to…. Not just to build his brand, or his companies, but to truly make people better.  At the core, this really matters. I will never doubt a human being that goes to these lengths, every single day, to show up.  Another reason why I’m
a Faithful Pheasant maxi and I’m never leaving. 

So grateful for your influence, all these years, G. ❤️ PS: Sales have been good! :)

text:
Grok give me the likely scenarios and the odds for what will happen in a 2029 election... 

5/4 – Hung parliament, Labour largest party, left-leaning government formed.
Labour + Lib Dems + Greens + SNP/Plaid (or similar “rainbow” arrangement). 
This is the central outcome in recent MRP modelling. The right’s vote is split between Reform, Restore and Conservatives, while the centre-left is more efficient under FPTP. 

7/4 – Restore and Reform split the right-wing vote and Labour (or a left coalition) forms the government.
Essentially the same as above but emphasising the split as the decisive factor. Restore is already taking 10-15%+ of 2024 Reform voters in some polls and has branches in hundreds of seats. Even 4-7% nationally can cost Reform 50-70 seats in marginals. 

4/1 – Reform wins most seats but only a minority government with limited power.
Reform edges Labour in seats (possible if Restore fades or they squeeze the Tories harder) but falls well short of 326. Relies on Conservative confidence-and-supply or informal deals; historically unstable and hard to pass any controversial legislation.

5/1 – Reform and Restore strike an electoral pact or post-election coalition and the right wins comfortably.
Lowe has publicly offered co-operation on hard-right policies (mass deportations etc.). A non-aggression pact in key seats could add dozens of seats for the combined right. Polling suggests a formal pact also risks putting off some 2024 Conservative-to-Reform switchers, so it is not cost-free. 

8/1 – Conservatives recover to become largest party or form a government.
Possible if Burnham’s government struggles, Reform/Restore self-destruct, and Kemi Badenoch (or successor) reunites enough of the right. They are currently projected second in seats despite third in votes. Big swing required from here.

10/1 – Labour wins an overall majority.
Requires Burnham to convert the current “bounce” into a 2024-style landslide and the right to remain fragmented. Possible but not the central forecast.

12/1 – Reform wins an overall majority.
Was the story in 2025 MRP polls (Reform ~311 seats). Now looks much harder because of Restore’s emergence and Labour’s recovery.

25/1 – Messy hung parliament with no stable government for months.
No combination can command a working majority; repeated failed Queen’s Speeches or a second election within a year.

33/1 – Your Party or another explicitly socialist/left-of-Labour force becomes a significant parliamentary player.
Currently polling at or near zero. Would need a major Labour collapse plus Green/Your Party surge.

50/1 – Greens become the largest party or lead a government.
Greens are competitive in some urban seats and polling in double digits nationally, but FPTP still heavily penalises them. Winning even 30-40 seats would be a historic result; becoming the biggest party is extreme.

100/1 – Conservatives win an overall majority.
Would require a dramatic reversal of 2024 + current trends.

200/1 – Restore Britain wins more than a handful of seats and becomes a kingmaker in its own right.
They are currently projected to hold Great Yarmouth and little else. Organisation and candidate quality remain unproven at national scale. 

The two most likely outcomes are variations of a Labour-led hung parliament caused in part by the Reform–Restore split. Everything else requires bigger shifts in the next 2–3 years. Odds will move with by-elections, local results, economic performance, and whether Farage and Lowe ever do a deal.

text:
My Sister Moved In to Help Me After Surgery, Then I Found Her in My Husband's Bed

The doctor said I needed six weeks to recover. My husband, James, said he'd take care of me. My sister, Natalie, offered to move in and help. I thought I was lucky. I had no idea I was inviting the devil into my home.

The surgery was on my spine. I couldn't walk, couldn't cook, couldn't even shower alone. Natalie was a godsend. She made meals. She cleaned. She helped me to the bathroom. She sat with me when James was at work. She was patient. Kind. Loving.

Or so I thought.

It started with small things. She wore my perfume. She borrowed my robe. She asked James for help with things she could easily do herself. I didn't think anything of it. She was my sister. I trusted her.

Then one night, I woke up at 2 a.m. in pain. I reached for my painkillers on the nightstand. They weren't there. I remembered I'd left them in the kitchen. I didn't want to wake James. He had work in the morning. So I grabbed my walker and slowly made my way down the hall.

The kitchen light was off. But I heard whispers. Coming from the guest room. Natalie's room.

I stopped. The door was slightly open. I peeked inside.

Natalie was in bed. James was beside her. They were both naked. His arm was around her. She was laughing softly.

I couldn't breathe. I couldn't move. I just stood there, my body trembling, my heart shattering into a million pieces.

text:
MADRID — More than 350 writers and other cultural figures have signed a petition defending the author Ariana Harwicz, who was disinvited from a literary festival in Spain over her support for Israel.

The Jewish-Argentinian novelist, longlisted for the 2018 Man Booker International Prize, was scheduled to participate in a talk on Sept. 26 at the Cultur Alh festival for arts and literature at the University of Granada. The festival organizers canceled her talk and rescinded her invitation after university activists complained about Harwicz’s views. The university said it was not involved in disinviting Harwicz and criticized the decision.

Harwicz vocally opposes cultural boycotts against Israeli writers and artists, which she describes as “antisemitism.” She has also dismissed accusations of genocide against Israel. The Spanish government is among Europe’s staunchest critics of Israel, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called Israel a “genocidal state.” The International Court of Justice is adjudicating accusations of genocide against Israel and has not issued a final ruling.

Harwicz received support from 352 cultural figures in a letter published on Wednesday. The signatories — including the Spanish philosopher Fernando Savater; the former French prime minister Manuel Valls, who is French-Spanish; and several prize-winning writers — called on the festival to explain its decision and offer Harwicz public redress. The renowned Irish writer John Banville, who was set to headline the event, dropped out after Harwicz’s cancellation.

The signatories said that the festival was denying “pluralism” and “the freedom to dissent.”
Shira Li Bartov, Jewish Telegraphic Agency

text:
🚛 Tesla Semi Is Finally in Production and Reaching Customers

After years of delays, Tesla’s long-awaited electric Semi truck is finally in volume production and beginning to reach customers this week. The company has spent the past three years refining the truck, reducing its weight and building a dedicated Semi factory next to its Gigafactory in Sparks, Nevada.

Tesla revealed the final production design in February 2026, confirming two versions: a Standard Range model rated for about 325 miles at the full 82,000-pound gross combination weight, and a Long Range version rated for 500 miles. The first production Semi rolled off the new line in April.

Tesla says the truck now consumes roughly 1,700 Wh per mile, an improvement over its original 2,000 Wh/mile target. The efficiency gains allow the company to use a smaller and lighter battery while maintaining the same range.

The Semi has also gone through a major powertrain redesign. Tesla replaced the earlier carbon-fiber-sleeved rotor with a steel-caged design, added a bar-wound stator shared with the Cybertruck, and developed a lighter drive axle.

Tesla argues that the Semi can offer lower operating costs than diesel trucks because of reduced energy expenses and fewer mechanical parts to maintain. With U.S. diesel prices remaining high, the company is positioning the truck as both an environmental and economic alternative for freight operators.

Now comes the real test: whether Tesla can ramp production reliably, deliver enough trucks to major fleet customers, and prove that the Semi’s range, charging performance and operating costs hold up in everyday freight service.

text:
SAME OUNCE, OPPOSITE YEARS: GOLD IS UP ABOUT 6% IN RUPEES AND DOWN ABOUT 6% IN WON:

Gold futures for December delivery at $4,320.50 an ounce, +$22.50 / +0.52% on Friday. Counted in dollars, gold's 2026 is a flat year: SPDR Gold Shares (GLD) at $393.41, +$1.72 / +0.44% on Friday, is down 0.7% since December 31 and about a fifth under its January 29 record. Asia's biggest buyers did not live that year. Priced in their own money since the end of 2025:
- India, in rupees: up about 6%
- Japan, in yen: about flat
- China, in yuan: down about 5%
- South Korea, in won: down about 6%

The verdict: the currency, not the metal, set what Asia paid for gold this year. The dearer price has pushed India's shoppers away. The cheaper one has not pulled China's shoppers in. The buyer stepping up is China's central bank.

How the math works: gold trades worldwide in dollars, so a shopper in Mumbai pays the dollar price times the exchange rate. When the rupee falls, Indian gold gets dearer even if the dollar price never moves. The rupee is down 6.3% against the dollar this year, to 95.8 per dollar, within about 1% of its weakest ever, near 97. India imports most of its oil, the Iran war has kept oil expensive, and foreign investors have sold a record amount of Indian stocks this year. All three mean more rupees sold for dollars.

The won went the other way. In early June it took about 1,560 won to buy a dollar; on Friday, 1,355. Foreign money pouring into Korea's chip stocks drove much of that, and earlier this month the won touched about 1,335, its strongest since October 2024. The yuan closed Monday at 6.695 per dollar, its strongest since July 2022, and last traded Thursday at 6.711, before China's markets shut Friday for the Mid-Autumn Festival.

India shows what a dearer price does. The local price peaked in August at 158,854 rupees per 10 grams, +12% in the month, then slipped 4.6% into mid-September, per the World Gold Council, an industry group. Shoppers waited. On September 11, Indian dealers were selling gold $78 an ounce under the official landed price - the cost of importing it, duty included - nearly 2% off, up from a $34 discount in July. August gold imports fell to $2.3B, -58% from a year earlier.

China shows a cheaper price is not enough. The strong yuan shaved August's rally: gold +13% in dollars on London's benchmark price, +8.4% in yuan on Shanghai's. Shoppers pulled back anyway. Withdrawals from the Shanghai Gold Exchange's vaults, the usual gauge of physical buying, were 62 tonnes in August, -27% from a year earlier, as jewelers faced higher prices and a tax change that raised their costs. The People's Bank of China did the opposite: 20.2 tonnes added in August, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023 and its 22nd straight month of buying, for 2,387 tonnes in reserve.

Nothing here trades again until Sunday evening, US time. The order, Eastern time:
- 6:00pm: gold and US stock futures reopen together. Where the stock futures stopped, each since Thursday's close: S&P 500 futures at 7,805.75, +38.75 / +0.50%; Nasdaq-100 futures at 30,921.75, +155 / +0.50%; Dow futures at 52,180.00, +463 / +0.90%.
- 8:00pm: Tokyo, where the Nikkei 225 ended Friday at 66,364, +850 / +1.30%.
- 9:00pm: the Shanghai Gold Exchange, shut since Thursday afternoon Beijing time, catches up on Friday's gain in dollars.
- 9:30pm: Hong Kong, where the Hang Seng ended Friday at 24,510, -251 / -1.01%, and mainland stocks, where the Shanghai Composite last traded Thursday at 3,888.37, -48.15 / -1.22%.
- 11:30pm: India's commodity exchange, the week's first new rupee price for gold.

For US stocks, this split sends no direct signal. Friday's link is simpler: West Texas Intermediate crude, the US oil benchmark, settled at $92.44 a barrel, -$2.17 / -2.29% on Friday, while stocks and gold both rose. The 6pm reopening is the first price on any weekend answer from Washington to Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and anything Asia adds after that can fade before Monday's 9:30am ET open. For an American holding GLD, gold's year is the dollar year: flat.

The dates that could change the split:
- October 1-7: China's markets and its gold exchange close for National Day. The People's Bank of China's September reserve figures, usually published around the 7th, show whether the central bank kept buying in September.
- October 11: India's festival season opens with Navratri, running to Dhanteras on November 6 and Diwali on November 8, when buying gold is considered auspicious.

The tell for India is that $78 discount. If it shrinks toward zero before Dhanteras, shoppers are coming back at a price that is still up for them this year. If it widens, the rupee has priced them out.

Gold gets sold as protection. This year it protected India's savers from a falling rupee, lost money for Korea's and China's savers in a year their own currencies did the protecting, and gave Americans nothing either way. Whether it worked depends on which currency pays you.

text:
⚠️ 🇮🇷 🇺🇸 Trump Rejects Iran’s Seven-Day Hormuz Offer, Keeps Pressure On Until After the Midterms

President Donald Trump has turned down Tehran’s latest bid to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in a week and pause regional fighting, according to The Wall Street Journal, while privately telling aides that renewed American strikes after November’s congressional elections remain on the table.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday that Tehran had sent a plan through Qatari mediators: if Washington showed seriousness, a deal would start a seven-day countdown to reopen the waterway and halt hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. In return, Iran wanted the United States to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, unfreeze assets, and ease oil sanctions. A U.S. official told Reuters that talks through mediators had been “positive and constructive.” Trump, the Journal reported, was privately unconvinced that Iran would meet his core demands.

Those demands have not changed. The president has insisted that any settlement address Iran’s nuclear program rather than park it until after a cease-fire. Earlier this week he told world leaders in New York that electoral politics would not drive his Iran policy. “The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” he said. Officials cited by the Journal added that he has told staff a renewed bombing campaign looks more likely than a deal that leaves Tehran’s enrichment path intact.

The scale of any post-election strikes is still undefined. Officials said Trump is wary of another major campaign in part because the United States wants to conserve munitions for other contingencies. They also cautioned that his view can shift as the midterms approach and as Iran’s behavior on the water changes.

The fight over Hormuz is now seven months old. The war opened on February 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes. A June memorandum of understanding briefly restored some shipping and was sold in Washington as a way to bring down energy prices without a forever war. That framework collapsed amid disputes over who would control the strait, Iranian attacks on commercial vessels, and American restoration of the blockade. Tehran has treated the chokepoint as leverage. Washington has treated free navigation and a verifiable nuclear limit as non-negotiable.

Trump’s refusal to take the seven-day package at face value fits that pattern. Iran’s offer would reopen a lane that carries a large share of the world’s oil, but only after the United States surrendered the economic pressure that has squeezed the regime. Accepting it on Tehran’s timetable would have locked in a pause before the nuclear file was settled. Holding the line until after November leaves the administration room to judge whether Iran is bargaining or buying time.

Gasoline prices and shipping risk remain the domestic cost of that stance. Trump has argued that the pain is temporary and that oil will fall once Iran can no longer use the strait as a weapon. Whether that happens through a tougher deal or through force after the midterms is the choice he has now signaled he is prepared to keep open.

The offer wasn't a simple weeklong truce. Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz only at the end of day seven, and only if the U.S. lifted its naval blockade, released over $12 billion in frozen assets, waived oil sanctions and agreed to a ceasefire on all fronts, including Lebanon.

Araghchi said the terms go no further than the Islamabad memorandum both sides signed in June, which fell apart in July after fighting broke out over the strait.

Analysts say Washington sees its blockade as working, leaving little incentive to revive terms it signed in June.

Both sides have alternated stalling since February: Trump has repeatedly set escalation deadlines and pulled them back, and Iran is now re-offering terms that already collapsed.

In public, Trump told the UN on Sept. 22 he believes a deal will come right after the election. In private, officials said he doubts Iran will meet his demands.

The report puts a date on the end of the stall: after November. But the officials who spoke to the WSJ said Trump is reluctant to resume major combat, the scope of any strikes is unclear, and his thinking could shift depending on the midterm results.

The rejection came days after Araghchi met Witkoff and Kushner in Qatar-mediated talks in New York, which a White House official had called positive and constructive.

text:
🧠🏆 What can be harder than solving a difficult mathematical problem?

It may be figuring out how to connect the people, skills, and effort needed to take on that challenge.

🌌🔍 The Justin Sun Prize offers an interesting perspective: the idea of “designing collaboration around knowledge.”

When we hear “prize system,” we often imagine a mechanism that simply rewards the person who achieves the result.

But a different perspective reveals something deeper.

💡 Not only “Who solved it?”
💡 But also “Who needs to act next to bring the result closer to completion?”
💡 And “How can different areas of expertise be connected toward one shared goal?”

These questions extend beyond mathematics.

They are also relevant when thinking about the open digital economy and blockchain infrastructures such as TRON. 🌐🔗

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🏆🧩 Justin Sun Prize: Thinking of Rewards as a Way to Bring People Together
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

According to Justin Sun’s explanation, the Justin Sun Prize is intended to recognize contributions to unsolved mathematical problems, including not only solving problems but also transforming proofs into forms that machines can verify.

What is particularly interesting is that the reward is not simply placed after the final achievement.

It can potentially become a reason for people with different abilities to participate.

The ability to solve a mathematical problem and the ability to formalize a proof may overlap, but they are not necessarily the same skill.

Someone discovers the breakthrough. 💡
Someone organizes the logic. 🧠
Someone tackles the difficult parts of formalization. 🔬
Someone completes the process toward machine verification. 🤖

Sometimes, a result can only move to the next stage when all of these contributions are connected. 🔗🤝

If rewards were linked only to the person who ultimately solved the problem, other work necessary to complete the result might receive less recognition.

The Justin Sun Prize’s description distinguishes between roles such as the Prover and the Formalizer, presenting formalization as an independent form of contribution.

This suggests that the role of a reward is not simply to celebrate effort.

A reward can also draw attention to stages where people are still needed and create a reason for someone to participate. 🌱

Of course, simply offering a reward does not guarantee that the necessary people will appear.

The difficulty of the task, required expertise, clarity of conditions, and evaluation process all matter.

Even so, clearly showing where contributions are possible and what needs to be achieved can provide important information for potential participants.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🧭🌱 Designing a Meeting Point Between “People Who Want to Participate” and “Work That Needs to Be Done”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

From a broader perspective, the Justin Sun Prize can also be viewed as a form of matching people with challenges in the world of knowledge.

People do not necessarily participate in research or development for the same reasons.

Some want to solve new problems. 💡
Others want to organize existing achievements. 📚
Some want to tackle technical challenges. 🛠️
Others find value in turning existing results into forms that are easier for others to use. 🌐

But if the work a project needs and the areas where participants can apply their strengths are not visible, the two sides may never meet. 🔍

That is why making unfinished work visible can be meaningful.

What has already been achieved?
What remains?
What role is needed next?
What conditions determine whether that work is complete?

When these elements are organized, potential contributors can more easily ask themselves:

“Is there something I can do here?” 📋✨

The goal is not simply to increase the number of participants.

It is to connect the work that needs to be done with the people who can contribute to it.

This perspective also applies to open development and Web3 ecosystems.

Even when the door is open to everyone, participation may not turn into concrete action if people cannot understand what they can contribute.

Conversely, when challenges, roles, and completion conditions are visible, participants can decide how to contribute according to their own skills and available time. 🌐🤝

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
⏳🔄 How Should We Handle the “Time Gap” Between Creating a Result and Completing It?
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

According to the explanation of the Justin Sun Prize, even after the mathematical community accepts a proof, machine verification may still be incomplete.

In such a case, the Prover’s contribution can be recorded while the Formalizer role remains open, with the reward held until formalization and verification are completed.

This reflects an important idea:

The moment a human proof is accepted and the moment that proof becomes fully machine-verifiable are not necessarily the same moment. 🧠⏳

Human acceptance does not automatically complete machine verification.

But that does not mean the contribution already achieved should be erased.

Instead, the remaining work can be made visible and connected toward completion. 🔗🌱

This is also interesting from a project-management perspective.

If every result is classified simply as “complete” or “incomplete,” it can become difficult to see the value of work already completed or understand what needs to happen next.

But when the state of each stage is visible, progress and remaining challenges can be considered separately.

This is more than a progress indicator.

It is a design that records what has already been contributed while leaving room for the next person to continue the work. 🌱

Of course, visibility does not make the remaining work easy.

The difficulty and time required for formalization can vary from problem to problem.

Still, clearly showing an intermediate state can provide an important foundation for continued collaboration.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
💰🔍 Reward Design Reveals “What We Choose to Value”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

A prize system is shaped not only by the size of its reward, but also by what it defines as a valuable contribution.

Does it reward only the final result?
Does it record important contributions along the way?
Does it recognize the work required to verify the result?
How clearly are the conditions for success defined?

These design choices tell participants what kinds of work are considered valuable. 📚

The Justin Sun Prize’s explanation includes not only solving problems but also transforming proofs into machine-verifiable forms.

This suggests attention not only to visible breakthroughs, but also to the work required to bring those breakthroughs closer to a state where they can be independently checked.

However, expanding the range of recognized contributions does not automatically guarantee fairness.

How are contribution boundaries defined?
What standards determine whether a result is accepted?
When multiple people contribute, how are their roles recorded?

To understand the system, we need to examine these conditions—not just the reward amount. ⚖️

According to Justin Sun’s explanation, prize problems are intended to be added to an official registry, with provisions intended to prevent published problems from being removed, alongside a policy that funds are designated for prize payments.

This raises a broader question:

How can the stability of the conditions be maintained before participants begin their work?

It is important to note that these points describe the stated design principles. They do not mean that every aspect of the actual implementation or operation has been independently verified.

Principles and implementation should be considered separately. 🔐

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🌐🔗 Viewing the Potential of TRON Through This Perspective
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

From here, I want to consider TRON through a slightly different lens.

Rather than viewing blockchain value only as the ability to process transactions, we can also view it as a common infrastructure through which different people and services can operate.

TRON supports digital-asset transfers and smart contracts.

On top of the network, not only tokens but also applications and various services can be built, allowing users to interact with the network for different purposes. 🌐

The important point is that the existence of infrastructure and the emergence of diverse activity on that infrastructure are two different stages.

What can developers build? 🛠️
Why do users choose to use it? 👤
How do services support user behavior?
How clearly can users understand the rules and conditions?

When these elements come together, a network can move beyond being merely a technical specification and become a practical set of options supporting real activity. 🌍✨

This does not mean that the Justin Sun Prize and TRON have direct technical integration.

The connection here is conceptual:

How can different contributions and activities be connected within a shared system?

The Justin Sun Prize attempts to connect contributions to knowledge through challenges, roles, and completion conditions.

A blockchain infrastructure such as TRON supports the use of assets and applications through network functionality and rules.

The systems are different.

But in both cases, understanding “what participants can do” and “under what conditions they can participate” is important. 🔗✨

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🧠📊 Look Beyond the Number of Users—Look at What Participation Actually Means
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

When examining Web3 projects, it is easy to focus on visible numbers such as user counts and transaction volume.

Of course, these numbers are useful for understanding network activity.

But without examining the behavior behind those numbers, it can be difficult to fully understand what that activity actually means.

Why are users participating?
Is there a reason to keep using the network?
What kinds of services are developers building?
Are the conditions and costs understandable for users?

Looking at the behavior behind the numbers allows us to think more concretely about what kinds of use cases a network actually supports. 🔍📈

For TRON, it is therefore important to observe not only network scale and processing capacity, but also actual transfers, digital-asset activity, application usage, and developer activity as distinct elements.

At the same time, network usage, TRX demand, and TRX market price are not the same thing.

We need to distinguish:

🔹 How usage affects demand for network resources
🔹 How it may affect TRX’s economic role
🔹 How supply dynamics interact with usage
🔹 How broader market conditions influence price

These factors should be analyzed separately.

This careful approach is not about denying TRON’s potential.

It is about understanding utility and economic effects without automatically treating them as the same thing. 🌐📊

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🚀🌱 Web3 Growth Depends on Designing Connections Between Participants
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

One idea that emerges from the Justin Sun Prize is the importance of creating roles and opportunities not only for people who produce the final result, but also for those who help bring that result toward completion.

The challenge is visible. 🔍
The required role is clear. 🧩
Contribution conditions are defined. 📋
Progress is recorded. 📝
The next participant can continue the remaining work. 🌱

This chain of steps can be viewed as an attempt to make collaboration easier to enter rather than leaving it entirely to goodwill or coincidence. 🤝

The same principle can apply to Web3 ecosystems, including TRON.

Beyond the technology itself, it matters what developers and users can actually do, under what conditions they can participate, and how their activity can create further value.

Technology alone does not automatically create adoption.

There needs to be a reason to participate.
The system needs to be understandable.
There needs to be a useful experience.
And that experience needs to create opportunities for further use and development. 🌍✨

These accumulated connections are what gradually shape the practical utility of a network.

🏆🌌 The Justin Sun Prize raises a question that goes beyond the size of its reward:

“HOW DO WE DISCOVER VALUABLE CONTRIBUTIONS, RECOGNIZE THEM, AND CONNECT THEM TO THE NEXT PERSON?” 🔍🔗🌱

That question applies not only to the world of knowledge, but also to the open digital economy.

🌐 When considering the potential of TRON, we should therefore look beyond functions and numbers alone.

We should also ask:

🔍 What activities does the infrastructure support?
👥 Who can participate?
🛠️ What can developers build?
🌱 What kinds of usage can emerge?
🔗 And what new activity can that usage enable?

A foundation for transferring value. 💸
An environment for creating services. 🛠️
A system through which participants can contribute. 🤝
And room for the next wave of use and creation. 🚀

The important question is how these elements connect.

And the answer should be explored not only through concepts, but by examining the actual mechanisms, conditions, and real-world usage behind them. 🔍📊🌐

🧠 Discover knowledge.
🔍 Make results verifiable.
🤝 Connect different contributions.
🌐 Build infrastructure people can actually use.
🌱 Leave room for the next participant.
🚀 Turn participation into the next possibility.

🧠✨ One of the most interesting developments around TRON is not a new token feature or another DeFi product.

It is the attempt to redesign how mathematical knowledge itself can be rewarded.

On September 16, 2026, Justin Sun announced the Justin Sun Prize, a mathematics prize built around a simple principle:

Proved, then paid.

Instead of making recognition depend primarily on annual ceremonies, nominations, age limits, or institutional affiliation, the Prize focuses on something much more objective: can the mathematical result be formally verified by a machine? 🔬💻

That seemingly small change creates a much larger idea.

📐 Mathematics has always been one of the hidden foundations of the digital economy. Cryptography, blockchain, secure computation and much of modern computer science ultimately depend on mathematical structures that must remain correct regardless of who uses them.

Justin Sun’s own explanation goes even deeper: wealth generated from a world built on mathematical foundations can be redirected toward advancing mathematics itself.

That is the philosophy behind the Justin Sun Prize.

🌐 And the mechanism is particularly interesting.

The Prize separates two kinds of work that are often treated as one.

① The Prover solves the mathematical problem.

② The Formalizer translates the proof into Lean so that the result can be checked in a machine-verifiable form.

The distinction matters.

A brilliant mathematical proof and the painstaking work required to turn that proof into something a computer can verify are different contributions. The Prize therefore allocates 70% of the reward to the solver and 30% to the Lean formalizer.

💡 This creates an incentive structure around a part of mathematics that has historically been valuable but comparatively difficult to monetize: formalization.

And this is where the concept becomes especially interesting in the AI era.

AI can generate ideas, explore enormous numbers of possibilities and assist with mathematical reasoning. But an AI-generated argument is not automatically a verified theorem.

The missing bridge is formal verification.

Lean provides that bridge by turning mathematical reasoning into a structure that a proof checker can examine step by step.

So the Prize is not simply paying people to solve difficult problems.

It is creating an economic incentive for converting human or AI-assisted reasoning into durable, machine-checkable knowledge. 🤖📐

That distinction could become increasingly important as AI systems become stronger.

📚 The current public problem bank contains 1,022 mathematical problems.

The early published material also highlights 66 records with detailed attribution information, while the broader catalog contains both open and solved problems.

This creates another interesting opportunity.

Some mathematical results already exist in papers and mathematical literature, yet their proofs have not necessarily been formalized in Lean.

In other words, solving a problem is not always the end of the journey.

There can still be an open slot between:

Human knowledge → formal specification → machine verification.

💎 The Justin Sun Prize puts a bounty on that missing step.

That changes the economics of formalization.

Instead of asking someone to spend weeks or months translating an existing proof into Lean purely for academic or open-source recognition, there can now be a clearly defined financial reward attached to completing the work.

The blank formalization field is therefore not merely an unfinished record.

It can become a visible inventory of valuable work waiting to be completed.

⛓️ This is also where the TRON connection becomes especially meaningful.

The Prize embraces an infrastructure philosophy familiar to blockchain:

Make the rules explicit.
Make the records public.
Make verification reproducible.
Make transactions independently observable.

Justin Sun has stated that the initial prize pool was transferred to the blockchain and that the address is public, allowing the balance to be inspected.

That matters because the promise of a reward becomes more credible when the underlying funds are not simply a number written on a webpage, but assets that can be publicly observed on-chain.

The Prize’s broader philosophy is therefore surprisingly close to the logic that made blockchain powerful in the first place.

Instead of asking:

Who should I trust?

The system increasingly asks:

What can be verified?

🔎 The application process follows the same direction.

A contribution is submitted, recorded through GitHub, subjected to verification and review, identity and payment requirements are completed, and the award is formally confirmed before payment.

The process is designed so that mathematical correctness is not determined simply by reputation.

The machine has to check the formal proof.

The community can examine the evidence.

And the blockchain can provide an independently observable record of the financial side.

That creates three different layers of verification:

📐 Mathematical verification
💻 Computational verification
⛓️ Financial transparency

This combination is what makes the Justin Sun Prize more interesting than a conventional sponsorship program.

It is an experiment in building an incentive system where knowledge, software verification and programmable financial infrastructure meet.

🌍 There is also a philosophical point here.

Traditional prizes generally recognize people after achievement has already become historically significant.

The Justin Sun Prize tries to create something closer to a live marketplace for unresolved intellectual work.

A problem is listed.
A bounty is attached.
Someone solves it.
Someone formalizes it.
A machine verifies it.
The record remains public.

The result is not just an award.

It is a public map of mathematical work that still needs to be completed or formalized.

And that idea feels particularly aligned with the evolution of Web3.

Web3 has always been about moving value and coordination from private institutions toward systems where rules, ownership and activity can be made more transparent and verifiable.

The Justin Sun Prize applies a similar mindset to something far outside finance:

knowledge itself. 🧠⛓️

For TRON, that is an important perspective.

TRON is often discussed through transactions, stablecoins, DeFi and digital assets. But the deeper theme is infrastructure: creating systems where digital value can move according to transparent, programmable rules.

The Justin Sun Prize extends that philosophy into philanthropy and research.

Money becomes an incentive.
GitHub becomes a public record.
Lean becomes a verification layer.
AI becomes a collaborator.
Blockchain becomes the transparency layer.

And the ultimate output is something that cannot be reduced to a transaction:

a mathematical proof that can remain verifiable long after the original participants are gone.

✨ That may be the most interesting part of the entire experiment.

A prize can disappear.
A company can disappear.
A trend can disappear.

But a correctly formalized theorem can remain.

The Justin Sun Prize is essentially attempting to connect financial incentives with that kind of permanence.

From a TRON perspective, this is worth watching closely.

Because the future of blockchain may not only be about moving money.

It may also be about building transparent systems for coordinating people, capital, computation and knowledge.

And the Justin Sun Prize is an unusually concrete example of that broader vision taking shape. 🌐💎🤖📐⛓️

She gained recognition for portraying Wonder Woman in the DC Extended Universe films (2016–2023). In 2018, Gadot was named one of Time's 100 most influential people in the world and ranked by Forbes as the tenth–highest-paid actress, later rising to third-highest in 2020. In 2025, she became the first Israeli actor to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.Gadot grew up in Rosh HaAyin and first gained attention locally after winning Miss Israel 2004, followed by two years of mandatory service in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) as a combat trainer. During this time, she participated in a Maxim photo shoot that boosted her public profile, leading her to begin modeling and endorsing various brands. Shortly after, she made her television debut in the Israeli drama Bubot in 2008, followed by her film debut in a supporting role as Gisele Yashar in Fast & Furious (2009), reprising it in multiple sequels (2011–2023). She also appeared on Israeli television in the second season of Asfur (2010–2012) and later in Kathmandu (2012).Gadot first portrayed Wonder Woman in Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice (2016). The success of the film led to her starring in Wonder Woman (2017), which became a major box office hit. She reprised the role again in Justice League (2017) and Wonder Woman 1984 (2020), the latter of which she co-produced. Since then, she has starred in Red Notice (2021), Death on the Nile (2022), and Heart of Stone (2023), which she co-produced. In 2025 she portrayed the Evil Queen in Snow White and Gemma Donati in In the Hand of Dante.Beyond acting, Gadot and her husband have co-founded a film production company, launched a food brand, and invested in Israeli startups. Gadot is widely celebrated in Israel as a national icon and ambassador and has been honored by various Jewish and Zionist organizations for her effect on Israel's image, including the Israeli-American Council (IAC), Anti-Defamation League (ADL), Jerusalem Film Festival, and Hadassah. She has also been awarded a Genesis Prize. Her support for the Israeli military and for hostages held in the Gaza Strip has drawn criticism from Palestinian nationalists, as well as from some pro-Israeli nationalists who argue she has not shown strong support.
Early life
Gadot was born on 30 April 1985[2] in Petah Tikva,[note 1] where she initially lived at Stampfer street.[9] She was born to Jewish parents of Ashkenazi descent;[7] her mother's roots are Czech and Polish, while her father's are Austrian, Russian, and German.[10] Her parents, Michael, an engineer, and Irit, a physical education teacher,[11][12] Hebraized their surname from "Greenstein" to "Gadot" before her birth.[13] In Hebrew, her first name means "wave", and her Hebrew surname 'Gadot' translates to "riverbanks".[6] She has a younger sister, Dana.[14]Her father was the sixth-generation of the Land of Israel/Palestine region and is an Israeli-born citizen,[15] and one of his ancestors was the first chemist at Shaare Zedek Hospital in Jerusalem,[16] while her mother is a first-generation Israeli-born citizen and the daughter of Holocaust survivors.[14][5] Her maternal grandfather,[5] Abraham Weiss,[17] was born as Adolf Weiss,[18] in the village of Munkács,[19] Czechoslovakia in 1928. At thirteen, when Nazi Germany invaded, his father (her great-grandfather) died in the army and Abraham, his mother, and his brother were sent to Auschwitz, where the latter two perished in the gas chamber. Gadot's maternal grandmother, however, managed to escape Europe before World War II.[20][15][17] Abraham immigrated alone to Jaffa, where he built a life. He later served in the Golani Brigade; in his later years, Abraham joined Israel Defense Forces (IDF) expeditions to give first-hand testimony about his experiences in Auschwitz.[21]In 1993, at age eight, Gadot and her family moved to the Givat Tal neighborhood of Rosh HaAyin, where she grew up,[22][8][15] in what she described as a "very Jewish, Israeli family environment".[14] As a child, she struggled with a weak voice and attended speech therapy, where she learned proper breathing techniques.[23] Encouraged by her mother to be active from a young age, Gadot took up swimming at four and later played tennis.[15] She joined the local volleyball and basketball teams,[24] soccer-team cheerleader,[19] and trained in ballet, hip-hop, and jazz for twelve years; at one point, she considered a career as a choreographer.[14]At eleven, Gadot visited Holocaust memorial sites in Poland to learn about Auschwitz and Majdanek. Reflecting on the experience, she recalled: "I, an entitled child, felt the suffering the Muselmann experienced back then."[25] At twelve, she was invited to enter the Girl of the Year [he] (Hebrew: נערת השנה) competition but declined, initially dismissed modeling as a career, but later realized it is a fun job that makes great money and offers exciting experiences.[24]Although Gadot's native language is Hebrew, she began taking English lessons in third grade; she became fluent after starting to watch the sitcoms Seinfeld and Friends.[26] She later attended Begin High School, where she majored in biology.[25] After graduating, she had a few months before beginning her mandatory two-year service in the IDF. During this time, she received modeling offers but instead chose to work at Burger King, saying, "I was like, posing for money? Ugh, it's not for me." Meanwhile, her mother and a friend submitted an application on her behalf for the Miss Israel pageant.[15] Before enlisting, she also worked as a caregiver for eight-month-old twins.[
